Using $-\partial(CV^2/2)/\partial\epsilon$ would omit the source work and reverse this sign.

For the independent stress calculation, the first-order potential suffices:
$$u=\frac1x+\epsilon\frac{f}{x^3}+O(\epsilon^2).$$
At $x_s=1+\epsilon f+O(\epsilon^2)$,
$$\left.\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right|_{x_s}=-1-\epsilon f+O(\epsilon^2).$$
Tangential coordinate components are $O(\epsilon)$ but affect the magnitude only at $O(\epsilon^2)$; the equipotential condition ensures that the field is normal to the actual surface. Hence
$$E_n=\frac{V}{a}(1+\epsilon f)+O(\epsilon^2),\qquad p=\frac{\epsilon_0V^2}{2a^2}(1+2\epsilon f)+O(\epsilon^2)\equiv p_0(1+2\epsilon f)+O(\epsilon^2).$$
The geometric factors needed for virtual work are
$$dA=a^2(1+2\epsilon f)d\Omega+O(\epsilon^2),$$
$$\boldsymbol n\cdot\frac{\partial\boldsymbol r_s}{\partial\epsilon}=a\left(f-\frac{2\epsilon}{5}\right)+O(\epsilon^2),$$
where $\boldsymbol n\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol r}=1+O(\epsilon^2)$. Therefore
$$\mathcal F_\epsilon^{({\rm stress})}=\oint p\,\boldsymbol n\cdot\frac{\partial\boldsymbol r_s}{\partial\epsilon}\,dA$$
$$=p_0a^3\int\left[f+\epsilon\left(4f^2-\frac25\right)\right]d\Omega+O(\epsilon^2)=p_0a^3\frac{8\pi}{5}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2),$$
so
$$\mathcal F_\epsilon^{({\rm stress})}=\frac{4\pi\epsilon_0aV^2}{5}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2).$$
This is the fixed-$V$ virtual-work result. For an isolated shell, $V=Q/C(\epsilon)=Q/C_0+O(\epsilon^2)$, so the same stress formula becomes
$$\mathcal F_\epsilon^{({\rm stress})}=\frac{Q^2}{20\pi\epsilon_0a}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2),$$
which agrees with the fixed-$Q$ calculation. Maxwell stress depends on the instantaneous field, not on which external apparatus maintains the state; the ensemble distinction enters when field and source energy are varied. A uniform mechanical pressure enforcing the volume constraint can cancel the inadmissible uniform expansion, but it performs no work on the admissible variation because $d\mathcal V/d\epsilon=0$ to the retained order. Finally, $p$ has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, while $p(a)(a^2)$ gives energy, as required for a force conjugate to dimensionless $\epsilon$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly enforces the volume constraint through second order, solves the displaced equipotential condition harmonic by harmonic, and obtains $g=-1/5$ and $C=4\pi\epsilon_0a(1+\epsilon^2/5)+O(\epsilon^3)$.
Derives both virtual-work forces with the correct signs and coefficients, including the fixed-voltage Legendre transform $G_V=-CV^2/2$ and an explicit voltage-source work balance.

Carries the Maxwell-stress calculation to the first nonzero order using the corrected pressure, area, and normal displacement; demonstrates ensemble agreement and correctly audits the constraint reaction, dimensions, and destabilizing sign.

commonErrors.description: Treating the stored field energy $CV^2/2$ as the complete mechanical potential when the voltage is held fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The ideal source's work is omitted, so the fixed-voltage generalized force is assigned the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Using only $\langle P_2\rangle=0$ to claim volume preservation, or dropping the second-order radial correction and first-order geometric factors in the stress integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The leading nonzero virtual work is either missed entirely or given an incorrect coefficient, preventing agreement with the capacitance calculation.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\int P_2d\Omega=0$, the surface $r=a(1+\epsilon P_2)$ already preserves volume. Taking $C=C_0(1+\epsilon^2/5)$, the fixed-voltage force follows from the stored energy as $\mathcal F_\epsilon=-d(CV^2/2)/d\epsilon=-C_0V^2\epsilon/5$. In the stress method the spherical pressure is uniform, so $\delta W=p_0a^3\delta\epsilon\int P_2d\Omega=0$. Thus the voltage source produces an inward generalized force, whereas the Maxwell stress gives no force on an isolated shell.

problems.title: Neutral Point–Cloud Composite: Multipoles, Boundaries, and Renormalized Energy
problems.objective: Analyze a compact neutral charge distribution containing a point singularity and a regular volume component, connecting distributional charge audits, multipole asymptotics, boundary regularity, and a controlled point-self-energy subtraction.
problems.statement:
Let $q>0$, $a>0$, and $0<d<a$. Consider the compactly supported charge distribution
$$\rho(\boldsymbol r)=q\,\delta^{(3)}(\boldsymbol r-d\hat{\boldsymbol z})-\frac{15q}{8\pi a^3}\left(1-\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)\Theta(a-r).$$
The potential vanishes at infinity. (a) Verify neutrality and derive the potential $\phi_s(r)$ of the regular, spherically symmetric component both inside and outside $r=a$. Audit the point singularity by computing the flux through a small sphere centered at $d\hat{\boldsymbol z}$. (b) Obtain an exact expression for the total potential when $r>a$, and derive its far-field expansion through quadrupole order. Identify the first two nonzero multipoles and explain why neutrality alone does not make the exterior field vanish. (c) Let $\boldsymbol E$ be the total field away from the point charge and define, for $0<\varepsilon<a-d$,
$$U_\varepsilon=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3\setminus B_\varepsilon(d\hat{\boldsymbol z})}|\boldsymbol E|^2d^3r.$$
Show that its only divergent term is $q^2/(8\pi\epsilon_0\varepsilon)$ and evaluate
$$U_{\rm reg}=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\left[U_\varepsilon-\frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0\varepsilon}\right].$$
The subtraction convention sets the isolated point charge's finite self-energy to zero. (d) At $r=a$, audit the continuity of the potential and its first two radial derivatives, explaining which continuity is required by the absence of a surface delta function. Also audit the limits $d\to0$ and $d\to a^-$, convergence of the far-zone field energy, SI dimensions, and the scaling under $a\mapsto\lambda a$, $d\mapsto\lambda d$ with $q$ fixed.
permittedResults: Gauss's law may be used to determine the field and potential of the spherical volume component.
For $r>d$, $|\boldsymbol r-d\hat{\boldsymbol z}|^{-1}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}d^\ell P_\ell(\cos\theta)/r^{\ell+1}$.
Away from singularities, electrostatic energy may be evaluated from $U=(\epsilon_0/2)\int |\boldsymbol E|^2d^3r$; any singular boundary term or subtraction must be determined explicitly.
problems.strategy: Normalize the polynomial cloud first and use its enclosed charge to obtain a piecewise radial potential. Outside the support, combine the cloud monopole with the displaced point potential before expanding; this makes monopole cancellation transparent without discarding higher moments. For the energy, decompose the field into point and cloud pieces, isolate the point-field integral in a small spherical exclusion, and retain the full point–cloud cross term. Finish by testing matching data at the cloud boundary and by rescaling every length in the final expressions.
hints: For $x=r/a<1$, the cloud charge enclosed within radius $r$ is $Q_s(r)=-(q/2)(5x^3-3x^5)$.
Outside $r=a$, the cloud contributes exactly $-q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)$; cancel only the $\ell=0$ term of the displaced point charge's Legendre expansion.
In the energy expansion $|\boldsymbol E_p+\boldsymbol E_s|^2$, the cross term contributes $q\phi_s(d)$, not $q\phi_s(d)/2$; the factor $1/2$ is canceled by the two symmetric cross contributions.
problems.solution:
The regular component has total charge
$$Q_s=-\frac{15q}{8\pi a^3}4\pi\int_0^a\left(1-\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)r^2dr=-\frac{15q}{2a^3}\left(\frac{a^3}{3}-\frac{a^3}{5}\right)=-q.$$
Adding the point charge gives $Q_{\rm tot}=q+Q_s=0$. For $x=r/a<1$, its enclosed cloud charge is
$$Q_s(r)=-\frac{15q}{2a^3}\left(\frac{r^3}{3}-\frac{r^5}{5a^2}\right)=-\frac q2(5x^3-3x^5).$$
Gauss's law then yields
$$\boldsymbol E_s(r)=-\frac{q}{8\pi\epsilon_0a^2}(5x-3x^3)\hat{\boldsymbol r},\qquad r<a.$$
For $r>a$, $\boldsymbol E_s=-q\hat{\boldsymbol r}/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$. Matching to $\phi_s(\infty)=0$ and integrating the field gives
$$\phi_s(r)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{q}{32\pi\epsilon_0a}\left(15-10\dfrac{r^2}{a^2}+3\dfrac{r^4}{a^4}\right),&r<a,\\[6pt]-\dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r},&r\ge a.\end{cases}$$
Near the point, with $s=|\boldsymbol r-d\hat{\boldsymbol z}|$,
$$\phi=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0s}+\phi_s(d)+O(s),\qquad \boldsymbol E=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0s^2}\hat{\boldsymbol s}+O(1).$$
Thus a sphere of radius $s$ centered on the point has outward flux
$$\oint\boldsymbol E\cdot d\boldsymbol a=\frac{q}{\epsilon_0}+O(s^2),$$
which recovers the delta-function coefficient.

For $r>a>d$, the total potential is exactly
$$\phi(r,\theta)=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{|\boldsymbol r-d\hat{\boldsymbol z}|}-\frac1r\right).$$
The cloud cancels only the point charge's monopole. Expanding the remaining terms gives
$$\phi(r,\theta)=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{d\cos\theta}{r^2}+\frac{d^2}{2r^3}(3\cos^2\theta-1)+O\left(\frac{d^3}{r^4}\right)\right].$$
The dipole moment is
$$\boldsymbol p=qd\hat{\boldsymbol z},$$
and the next term is the axisymmetric quadrupole proportional to $qd^2P_2(\cos\theta)$. Zero total charge removes the $1/r$ term but places no requirement on these higher moments.

For the regularized energy, write $\boldsymbol E=\boldsymbol E_p+\boldsymbol E_s$. The point-field contribution outside an exclusion sphere is
$$\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_{s>\varepsilon}E_p^2d^3r=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}4\pi\int_\varepsilon^\infty\left(\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0s^2}\right)^2s^2ds=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0\varepsilon}.$$
The cloud field is bounded near the point, so its missing energy is $O(\varepsilon^3)$. The leading point–cloud cross integrand is proportional to $\hat{\boldsymbol s}\cdot\boldsymbol E_s(d)/s^2$, whose angular integral vanishes; the remaining cross integral has a finite limit. By electrostatic reciprocity or integration by parts,
$$\epsilon_0\int\boldsymbol E_p\cdot\boldsymbol E_s\,d^3r=q\phi_s(d).$$
There is therefore no further divergence. The cloud self-energy is
$$U_s=\frac12\int\rho_s\phi_s\,d^3r$$
$$=\frac{15q^2}{128\pi\epsilon_0a}\int_0^1x^2(1-x^2)(15-10x^2+3x^4)dx.$$
The integral is
$$\int_0^1(15x^2-25x^4+13x^6-3x^8)dx=\frac{32}{21},$$
so
$$U_s=\frac{5q^2}{28\pi\epsilon_0a}.$$
Writing $\eta=d/a$, the finite interaction energy is
$$q\phi_s(d)=-\frac{q^2}{32\pi\epsilon_0a}(15-10\eta^2+3\eta^4).$$
Accordingly,
$$U_{\rm reg}=U_s+q\phi_s(d)=\frac{q^2}{224\pi\epsilon_0a}\left(-65+70\eta^2-21\eta^4\right).$$
The interaction is not halved: in $\frac12\int\rho\phi$, the point in the cloud potential and the cloud in the point potential are equal contributions whose sum removes the prefactor $1/2$.

At the cloud boundary, direct evaluation gives
$$\phi_s(a^-)=\phi_s(a^+)=-\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0a},$$
$$\phi_s'(a^-)=\phi_s'(a^+)=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0a^2},$$
$$\phi_s''(a^-)=\phi_s''(a^+)=-\frac{q}{2\pi\epsilon_0a^3}.$$
Continuity of $\phi_s$ and its first normal derivative is required because there is neither an imposed potential jump nor a surface charge delta function at $r=a$. The second derivative also matches here because the volume density approaches zero at the boundary. The third derivative does not match: the inside and outside values are respectively $-9q/(4\pi\epsilon_0a^4)$ and $6q/(4\pi\epsilon_0a^4)$. The displaced point potential is analytic across $r=a$ and therefore does not alter any of these jumps.

As $d\to0$, every exterior multipole vanishes and the exact exterior potential becomes zero, as expected for a concentric, spherically symmetric neutral distribution. The regularized energy tends to
$$U_{\rm reg}\longrightarrow-\frac{65q^2}{224\pi\epsilon_0a}.$$
As $d\to a^-$,
$$U_{\rm reg}\longrightarrow-\frac{q^2}{14\pi\epsilon_0a}.$$
At large radius the leading field is dipolar, $E=O(r^{-3})$, so the field energy beyond radius $R$ behaves as $\int_R^\infty r^2r^{-6}dr=O(R^{-3})$ and converges. The density has SI units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, the potential has units $\mathrm V$, and $q^2/(\epsilon_0a)$ has units $\mathrm J$. Under $a\mapsto\lambda a$ and $d\mapsto\lambda d$ with $q$ fixed, $\eta$ is unchanged, an order-$\ell$ multipole moment scales as $\lambda^\ell$, the geometrically corresponding potential scales as $\lambda^{-1}$, and $U_{\rm reg}$ scales as $\lambda^{-1}$. Scaling the regulator as $\varepsilon\mapsto\lambda\varepsilon$ gives the same scaling for the subtracted singular term.
rubricCriteria: Correctly normalizes the regular cloud, derives its piecewise potential, verifies the point-source flux, and performs the $r=a$ matching audit with a correct explanation of which derivatives must be continuous.
Obtains the exact exterior potential and its dipole and quadrupole terms, explicitly distinguishing monopole cancellation from complete exterior-field cancellation and checking the concentric limit.

Isolates the precise $q^2/(8\pi\epsilon_0\varepsilon)$ divergence, evaluates both the cloud self-energy and the full point–cloud interaction, and supplies the requested endpoint, far-energy, dimensional, and dilation audits.

commonErrors.description: Inferring from zero total charge that Gauss's law forces the complete exterior field to vanish, without checking the displaced point charge's higher multipoles.
commonErrors.consequence: The dipole and quadrupole terms are lost, producing an incorrect far field and an incorrect far-zone energy scaling.

commonErrors.description: Substituting the point charge directly into $\frac12\int\rho\phi$ without isolating its singular self-field, or retaining only $q\phi_s(d)/2$ as the point–cloud interaction.
commonErrors.consequence: The self-energy is undefined or the finite regularized energy has an erroneous factor of two in its interaction term.

problems.flawedProof: The cloud has charge $-q$, so the total enclosed charge is zero and Gauss's law gives $\boldsymbol E=0$ for every $r>a$. For the energy, discard the infinite value of the point charge's own potential and use $U=\frac12\int\rho\phi\,d^3r$. This leaves $U_{\rm reg}=U_s+\frac12q\phi_s(d)$, because the point charge samples the finite cloud potential at its position.

problems.title: Complete a guided Dirichlet uniqueness argument
problems.objective: Use a supplied energy identity to show that fixed boundary potential determines a source-region solution uniquely.
problems.statement:
Two potentials $V_1,V_2$ satisfy the same Poisson equation in a bounded connected region $\Omega$ and the same value on its boundary. Set $u=V_1-V_2$. You may use Green's identity
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,d\tau=\oint_{\partial\Omega}u\,\partial_nu\,da-\int_\Omega u\nabla^2u\,d\tau.$$
Fill in the uniqueness proof. Then explain which step fails if only the normal derivative is prescribed. Finally test the argument on $u=C$, a nonzero constant.
permittedResults: Green's first identity is supplied.
problems.strategy: Subtract the two boundary-value problems, apply the supplied identity to the homogeneous difference, and interpret a zero integral of a nonnegative quantity.
hints: The difference obeys $\nabla^2u=0$.
Dirichlet data makes $u=0$ on the boundary.
If $\nabla u=0$ on a connected region, $u$ is constant.
problems.solution:
The difference satisfies $
abla^2u=0$ in $\Omega$ and $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Both terms on the right of Green's identity vanish, so
$$\int_\Omega|
abla u|^2d	au=0.$$
The continuous nonnegative integrand must vanish, hence $
abla u=0$. Connectedness makes $u$ constant, and its zero boundary value makes that constant zero. Thus $V_1=V_2$. With Neumann data, $\partial_nu=0$ kills the boundary term but only yields that $u$ is an arbitrary constant; $u=C
e0$ is exactly the surviving ambiguity.
rubricCriteria: Forms the harmonic homogeneous difference.
Uses both the PDE and boundary data to eliminate the energy-identity terms.
Explains the constant ambiguity for Neumann data with the requested test.

commonErrors.description: Concludes $u=0$ directly from $\nabla^2u=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Nonzero harmonic functions and the role of boundary data are ignored.

commonErrors.description: Claims homogeneous Neumann data also forces the constant to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The additive gauge freedom is incorrectly removed.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\nabla^2u=0$, the function itself must be zero. The same reasoning works for Neumann data, so $u=C$ is forbidden unless $C=0$.

problems.title: Check Neumann compatibility before solving
problems.objective: Derive the total-flux condition for a Neumann problem and distinguish incompatibility from additive-constant nonuniqueness.
problems.statement: In a bounded region, $V$ is to satisfy $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0$ and prescribed outward derivative $\partial_nV=g$ on the boundary. Integrate the equation to derive the compatibility condition relating $g$ and total charge. Decide whether a source-free unit cube can have $g=1\,\mathrm{V/m}$ on every face. If $g=0$ and $\rho=0$, explain why both $V=0$ and $V=7\,\mathrm V$ solve the problem and give one normalization that restores uniqueness.
permittedResults: Use the divergence theorem for $\nabla V$.
problems.strategy: Integrate before attempting separation, compare the prescribed net normal derivative with total charge, and treat constant shifts as gauge freedom rather than new fields.
hints: $\int_\Omega\nabla^2V=\oint g$.
For a source-free cube, the required net flux is zero.
A condition such as mean-zero potential fixes the constant.
problems.solution:
Integration gives
$$\boxed{\oint_{\partial\Omega}g\,da=-\frac1{\epsilon_0}\int_\Omega\rho\,d\tau}.$$
For a unit cube with $\rho=0$ and $g=1\,\mathrm{V/m}$ on all six outward faces, the left side is $6\,\mathrm{V\,m}$ rather than zero, so no solution exists. With homogeneous data, adding a constant changes neither $\nabla^2V$ nor $\partial_nV$, so $0$ and $7\,\mathrm V$ are both solutions. Requiring $\int_\Omega Vd\tau=0$ or fixing $V$ at one point removes the ambiguity.
rubricCriteria: Derives the compatibility condition with the Poisson sign.
Rejects the cube data using its nonzero net prescribed flux.
Separates constant nonuniqueness from incompatibility and supplies a valid normalization.

commonErrors.description: Checks Neumann data face by face but never checks its net flux.
commonErrors.consequence: An incompatible problem is treated as solvable.

commonErrors.description: Calls two constant-shifted potentials different electric fields.
commonErrors.consequence: Potential gauge freedom is confused with physical nonuniqueness.

problems.flawedProof: Each face condition is smooth, so a solution must exist. The constants $0$ and $7$ produce different electrostatic fields because their numerical potentials differ.

problems.title: One separated mode solves a rectangular Dirichlet problem
problems.objective: Construct and verify the single-mode Laplace solution generated by sinusoidal data on one side of a rectangle.
problems.statement: On $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, solve $\nabla^2V=0$ with $V(0,y)=V(a,y)=V(x,0)=0$ and $V(x,b)=V_0\sin(\pi x/a)$. Find $V$, compute $E_y$ at $(a/2,b/2)$, and verify every boundary value.
permittedResults: A separated harmonic mode may use $\sin(kx)\sinh(ky)$.
problems.strategy: Match the side zeros with a sine factor, choose the hyperbolic factor that vanishes at the bottom, and normalize at the top.
hints: The $x$ wavenumber is $k=\pi/a$.
Use $\sinh(ky)$ rather than $\cosh(ky)$.
$E_y=-\partial_yV$.
problems.solution:
With $k=\pi/a$,
$$\boxed{V(x,y)=V_0\sin(kx)\frac{\sinh(ky)}{\sinh(kb)}}.$$
It is harmonic because the $x$ and $y$ second derivatives cancel. The sine vanishes at $x=0,a$, the hyperbolic sine at $y=0$, and $y=b$ gives the prescribed top data. Moreover
$$E_y=-V_0k\sin(kx)\frac{\cosh(ky)}{\sinh(kb)},$$
so
$$\boxed{E_y(a/2,b/2)=-\frac{\pi V_0}{a}\frac{\cosh(\pi b/(2a))}{\sinh(\pi b/a)}}.$$
The units are volts per meter.
rubricCriteria: Chooses the separated factors that satisfy three grounded sides.
Normalizes exactly to the sinusoidal top boundary.
Differentiates with the correct electric-field sign and evaluates the requested point.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\cosh(ky)$ without subtracting a term at the grounded bottom.
commonErrors.consequence: The $y=0$ boundary is not zero.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor $1/\sinh(kb)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The top voltage has the wrong amplitude.

problems.flawedProof: Take $V=V_0\sin(\pi x/a)\cosh(\pi y/a)$. It is harmonic, so all boundary values automatically follow, and $E_y=+\partial_yV$.

problems.title: Use the half-plane Poisson kernel as a boundary-data filter
problems.objective: Apply a supplied Poisson-kernel formula to a single Fourier boundary mode and check its decay and boundary limit.
problems.statement:
For $y>0$, you may use the fact that boundary data $f(x)=V_0\cos(kx)$ has harmonic extension
$$V(x,y)=V_0e^{-|k|y}\cos(kx).$$
Verify directly that this solves Laplace's equation and tends to $f$ as $y\downarrow0$. Compute both electric-field components, their magnitude, and the flux through one wavelength of the line $y=h$ with upward normal. Explain why the net flux is zero although the local normal field is not.
permittedResults: The harmonic extension of the cosine mode is supplied.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the supplied extension rather than re-deriving the transform, then integrate the cosine normal field over exactly one period.
hints: For $k>0$, differentiate $e^{-ky}$.
Both field components have the same exponential scale.
The integral of cosine over a full wavelength is zero.
problems.solution:
Taking $k>0$ without loss of generality,
$$\partial_x^2V=-k^2V,\qquad\partial_y^2V=k^2V,$$
so $\nabla^2V=0$, and $V(x,0)=V_0\cos(kx)$. The field is
$$\boxed{E_x=kV_0e^{-ky}\sin(kx),\qquad E_y=kV_0e^{-ky}\cos(kx)}.$$
Thus $|\mathbf E|=k|V_0|e^{-ky}$. Upward flux per unit transverse length through one period is
$$\int_0^{2\pi/k}E_y(x,h)dx=kV_0e^{-kh}\int_0^{2\pi/k}\cos(kx)dx=0.$$
Positive and negative local flux regions cancel.
rubricCriteria: Verifies harmonicity and the boundary limit from the supplied mode.
Computes both field components and the constant-in-$x$ magnitude.
Shows cancellation of normal flux over one full period.

commonErrors.description: Uses $e^{+ky}$ for the upper half-plane solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The solution grows away from bounded boundary data and violates the decay condition.

commonErrors.description: Infers zero local $E_y$ from zero period-averaged flux.
commonErrors.consequence: Pointwise field is confused with its integral.

problems.flawedProof: Because the boundary cosine averages to zero, its harmonic extension is zero for every $y>0$. Equivalently the normal field vanishes pointwise, not just after integration.

problems.title: Split a strip solution into a baseline and one correction mode
problems.objective: Use linearity to combine unequal constant plate potentials with a sinusoidal side perturbation in a rectangular strip.
problems.statement:
On $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, impose $V(x,0)=0$, $V(x,b)=V_b$, and
$$V(0,y)=\frac{V_b y}{b}+A\sin(\pi y/b),\qquad V(a,y)=\frac{V_b y}{b}.$$
Find the harmonic solution by separating a linear baseline from one correction mode. Verify all four sides and state what happens at the corners.
permittedResults: The linear function $V_by/b$ is harmonic.
problems.strategy: Remove the shared linear top-to-bottom profile, then solve the remaining left-driven sine mode with an $x$ factor that vanishes at the right wall.
hints: Set $V=V_by/b+u$.
For $u$, use $\sin(\pi y/b)$ and a hyperbolic function of $a-x$.
Normalize the correction at $x=0$.
problems.solution:
Let $k=\pi/b$. The solution is
$$\boxed{V(x,y)=\frac{V_by}{b}+A\sin(ky)\frac{\sinh(k(a-x))}{\sinh(ka)}}.$$
Both terms are harmonic. At $x=0$ the ratio is one; at $x=a$ it is zero. At $y=0,b$ the sine vanishes, leaving the required constant plate values. The side data agree at all four corners because the sine perturbation vanishes there, so no corner discontinuity is being hidden.
rubricCriteria: Identifies and removes the harmonic linear baseline.
Constructs and normalizes the left-driven sine correction.
Verifies all sides and explicitly audits corner compatibility.

commonErrors.description: Expands the constant top voltage entirely as a sine series without preserving its corner behavior.
commonErrors.consequence: The boundary interpretation becomes unnecessarily ambiguous at the corners.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\sinh(kx)$ for a correction that must vanish at $x=a$.
commonErrors.consequence: The right wall acquires an unwanted perturbation.

problems.flawedProof: Use $V=V_by/b+A\sin(\pi y/b)\sinh(\pi x/b)$. Since each factor is smooth, the right wall condition is automatically unchanged.

problems.title: Compute the first coefficients of a square-cavity voltage step
problems.objective: Project simple piecewise top-wall data onto sine modes and use the coefficients in the standard rectangular solution.
problems.statement:
A square $0<x<a$, $0<y<a$ is grounded on three sides. On the top, $V(x,a)=V_0$ for $0<x<a/2$ and $0$ for $a/2<x<a$. Use
$$V(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty B_n\sin(n\pi x/a)\frac{\sinh(n\pi y/a)}{\sinh(n\pi)}.$$
Find $B_n$, compute $B_1,B_2,B_3$, and write the three-mode approximation at the center. State why the boundary value at $x=a/2$ is interpreted by a limiting average.
permittedResults: For a sine series, $B_n=(2/a)\int_0^af(x)\sin(n\pi x/a)dx$.
problems.strategy: Project only over the energized half of the top wall, evaluate the elementary cosine endpoint, and substitute the center coordinates after finding coefficients.
hints: The integral ends at $a/2$.
At the center, use $\sin(n\pi/2)$ and $\sinh(n\pi/2)/\sinh(n\pi)$.
problems.solution:
Projection gives
$$\boxed{B_n=\frac{2V_0}{n\pi}\left[1-\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)\right]}.$$
Hence $B_1=2V_0/\pi$, $B_2=2V_0/\pi$, and $B_3=2V_0/(3\pi)$. At $x=y=a/2$, the even mode vanishes, so
$$V_3=\frac{2V_0}{\pi}\frac{\sinh(\pi/2)}{\sinh\pi} -\frac{2V_0}{3\pi}\frac{\sinh(3\pi/2)}{\sinh3\pi}.$$
At a jump, the Fourier series converges to the average of the two one-sided boundary values, here $V_0/2$; this isolated convention does not alter the interior harmonic solution.
rubricCriteria: Projects the step over the correct half interval.
Computes the first three coefficients and evaluates the center mode factors.
Explains the Fourier limiting value at the discontinuity without treating it as interior nonuniqueness.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the energized voltage over the full top wall.
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient formula describes a different boundary condition.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the $n=2$ mode at $x=a/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The center approximation ignores the sine factor's zero.

problems.flawedProof: Because the top is mostly constant, $B_n=2V_0/(n\pi)$ for every $n$. At the center all three sine factors equal one, so the first three modes add with positive signs.

problems.title: Final A: a mixed Cartesian mode with a uniqueness check
problems.objective: Solve a one-mode mixed Dirichlet-Neumann rectangle and verify both its numerical field value and uniqueness class.
problems.statement: On $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, solve $\nabla^2V=0$ with $V(0,y)=V(a,y)=0$, $\partial_yV(x,0)=0$, and $V(x,b)=V_0\sin(2\pi x/a)$. Find $V$. For $a=2.00\,\mathrm m$, $b=1.00\,\mathrm m$, and $V_0=10.0\,\mathrm V$, compute $E_y$ at $(a/4,b/2)$. Explain briefly why the mixed data determine a unique solution.
permittedResults: A zero normal derivative at $y=0$ selects a $\cosh(ky)$ factor.
problems.strategy: Use the prescribed sine mode in $x$, choose the even hyperbolic factor for the bottom Neumann condition, normalize at the top, and apply the homogeneous energy argument for uniqueness.
hints: Here $k=2\pi/a$.
Normalize by $\cosh(kb)$.
problems.solution:
The solution is
$$\boxed{V=V_0\sin(kx)\frac{\cosh(ky)}{\cosh(kb)},\qquad k=\frac{2\pi}{a}}.$$
It vanishes on the vertical sides, has $\partial_yV=0$ at the bottom, and matches the top. Moreover
$$E_y=-V_0k\sin(kx)\frac{\sinh(ky)}{\cosh(kb)}.$$
With $a=2$, $b=1$, $k=\pi\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, the requested point gives
$$\boxed{E_y=-10\pi\frac{\sinh(\pi/2)}{\cosh\pi}\approx-6.24\,\mathrm{V/m}}.$$
For the difference of two solutions, Green's identity has zero Dirichlet contribution on three boundary pieces and zero normal derivative on the fourth, forcing zero gradient and then zero constant from the Dirichlet sides.
rubricCriteria: Selects and normalizes the correct sine-cosh separated mode.
Computes the field with correct sign, units, and numerical substitution.
Applies the mixed homogeneous energy argument to justify uniqueness.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\sinh(ky)$ at the insulated bottom.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal derivative there is nonzero.

commonErrors.description: Uses $k=\pi/a$ despite the prescribed second sine mode.
commonErrors.consequence: The top boundary wavelength and numerical field are wrong.

problems.flawedProof: The bottom Neumann condition requires $V=0$ there, so use $\sinh(\pi y/a)$. The top sine has wavenumber $\pi/a$, giving a positive $E_y$ at the requested point.

problems.title: A regular cylindrical harmonic follows its boundary Fourier mode
problems.objective: Separate a two-dimensional cylindrical Laplace problem and select the radial branch regular at the axis.
problems.statement: Inside a long cylinder $s<a$, the boundary is held at $V(a,\phi)=V_0\cos(3\phi)$. There is no $z$ dependence. Find the potential and electric-field components. Check regularity at $s=0$ and compute the surface charge density on the inner face of the conducting wall, taking the normal from the cavity into the conductor.
permittedResults: For angular mode $m$, radial solutions are $s^m$ and $s^{-m}$.
problems.strategy: Match the angular cosine, discard the singular inverse-power branch, normalize at the wall, and differentiate in cylindrical coordinates.
hints: Use $m=3$.
$E_s=-\partial_sV$ and $E_\phi=-(1/s)\partial_\phi V$.
For the normal $\hat n=\hat s$ directed from cavity to metal, the boundary jump gives $\sigma=-\epsilon_0\mathbf E_{\rm cavity}\cdot\hat n$.
problems.solution:
Regularity removes $s^{-3}$, so
$$\boxed{V=V_0(s/a)^3\cos3\phi}.$$
The field is
$$E_s=-\frac{3V_0s^2}{a^3}\cos3\phi,\qquad E_\phi=\frac{3V_0s^2}{a^3}\sin3\phi.$$
Both components vanish at the axis, so the apparent angular coordinate ambiguity is harmless. With $\hat n=\hat s$ directed from cavity to metal, $\sigma=-\epsilon_0\mathbf E_{\rm cavity}\cdot\hat n$, and therefore
$$\boxed{\sigma(\phi)=-\epsilon_0E_s(a^-,\phi)=\frac{3\epsilon_0V_0}{a}\cos3\phi}.$$
Its integral around the wall is zero, consistent with a pure nonzero angular mode.
rubricCriteria: Selects the $s^3$ branch and normalizes it at the wall.
Computes both cylindrical field components correctly.
Uses the declared normal for the surface charge and checks its zero net value.

commonErrors.description: Retains the $s^{-3}$ branch inside the cylinder.
commonErrors.consequence: The source-free potential is singular at the axis.

commonErrors.description: Omits the $1/s$ factor in $E_\phi$.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular field has wrong units and radial scaling.

problems.flawedProof: Both $s^3$ and $s^{-3}$ are allowed because the boundary is finite. Also $E_\phi=-\partial_\phi V$, so it scales as $s^3$ and has units of volts.

problems.title: Match one Fourier mode across an annular cylinder
problems.objective: Solve the two-coefficient radial problem for one angular mode between concentric cylindrical boundaries.
problems.statement: In $a<s<b$, impose $V(a,\phi)=V_a\cos(2\phi)$ and $V(b,\phi)=V_b\cos(2\phi)$. Find $V(s,\phi)$ in the form $(As^2+B/s^2)\cos2\phi$ by solving for $A,B$. Verify both boundaries and state the regular solid-cylinder limit when $a\to0$ with bounded potential.
permittedResults: The $m=2$ radial basis is $s^2,s^{-2}$.
problems.strategy: Treat the two boundary values as a two-by-two linear system in $A$ and $B$, then diagnose the inner-radius limit from regularity rather than from formal substitution alone.
hints: Multiply the boundary equations by $a^2$ and $b^2$ if useful.
The determinant is $a^2/b^2-b^2/a^2$.
Boundedness at a restored axis forces $B=0$.
problems.solution:
The system $Aa^2+B/a^2=V_a$, $Ab^2+B/b^2=V_b$ gives
$$\boxed{A=\frac{V_bb^2-V_aa^2}{b^4-a^4}},\qquad \boxed{B=\frac{a^2b^2(V_ab^2-V_ba^2)}{b^4-a^4}}.$$
Substitution recovers both boundary amplitudes. If the inner boundary shrinks to an ordinary axis, boundedness requires $B=0$; compatible outer data then gives $V=V_b(s/b)^2\cos2\phi$. A fixed nonzero $V_a$ on a vanishing inner conductor does not define that regular limit.
rubricCriteria: Solves the two boundary equations for both radial coefficients.
Verifies the amplitudes at $a$ and $b$.
States the bounded-axis condition and the compatibility issue in the solid limit.

commonErrors.description: Drops the inverse-power branch merely because the domain is bounded.
commonErrors.consequence: The inner boundary condition cannot generally be satisfied in an annulus.

commonErrors.description: Takes $a\to0$ while retaining $B/s^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed solid-cylinder limit is singular at the axis.

problems.flawedProof: Because the region is inside the outer cylinder, regularity always removes $B/s^2$. Set $A=V_a/a^2=V_b/b^2$ even when the two prescribed voltages do not satisfy that relation.

problems.title: Normalize the first Fourier-Bessel mode in a finite cylinder
problems.objective: Use a supplied Fourier-Bessel basis and orthogonality norm to project simple endcap data onto its first modes.
problems.statement:
A cylinder $0<s<a$, $0<z<L$ is grounded at $s=a$ and $z=L$. At $z=0$, $V(s,0)=V_0(1-s^2/a^2)$. You may use
$$V=\sum_{n\ge1}A_nJ_0(j_{0n}s/a)\frac{\sinh[j_{0n}(L-z)/a]}{\sinh(j_{0n}L/a)}$$
and
$$\int_0^a sJ_0(j_{0n}s/a)^2ds=\frac{a^2}{2}J_1(j_{0n})^2.$$
Derive the coefficient integral for $A_n$, write $A_1$ explicitly as a one-dimensional integral, and verify the three grounded boundaries and axis regularity.
permittedResults: The separated basis and its diagonal norm are supplied.
problems.strategy: Project the endcap function with weight $s$, divide by the supplied norm, and audit boundary factors without attempting an unnecessary closed form for the remaining integral.
hints: Multiply the $z=0$ series by $sJ_0(j_{0m}s/a)$ and integrate.
Every $j_{0n}$ is a zero of $J_0$.
$J_0(0)=1$ is finite.
problems.solution:
Orthogonal projection gives
$$\boxed{A_n=\frac{2V_0}{a^2J_1(j_{0n})^2} \int_0^a s\left(1-\frac{s^2}{a^2}\right)J_0(j_{0n}s/a)\,ds}.$$
In particular this formula with $n=1$ is the requested $A_1$; equivalently, after $u=s/a$,
$$A_1=\frac{2V_0}{J_1(j_{01})^2}\int_0^1u(1-u^2)J_0(j_{01}u)du.$$
At $s=a$, every $J_0(j_{0n})=0$; at $z=L$, every hyperbolic numerator vanishes. At $z=0$ the ratio is one and orthogonal completeness restores the endcap data. At $s=0$, $J_0(0)=1$, so no axis singularity appears.
rubricCriteria: Uses the cylindrical weight $s$ in the projection.
Divides by the supplied Bessel norm and gives the requested first coefficient.
Verifies all grounded boundaries and axis regularity from the basis factors.

commonErrors.description: Projects using $ds$ rather than $s\,ds$.
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficients violate the Sturm-Liouville weight and do not reproduce the endcap data.

commonErrors.description: Uses zeros of $J_1$ at the side wall.
commonErrors.consequence: The Dirichlet condition $V(a,z)=0$ is not enforced.

problems.flawedProof: Ordinary Fourier orthogonality gives $A_n=\int_0^af(s)J_0(j_{0n}s/a)ds$. The side is grounded because $J_1(j_{0n})=0$, and the axis is singular because cylindrical coordinates fail there.

problems.title: Continue two Legendre boundary modes outside a sphere
problems.objective: Map prescribed axisymmetric spherical boundary data to its decaying exterior harmonic and induced surface field.
problems.statement: Outside a sphere $r>a$, let $V(a,\theta)=V_1\cos\theta+V_2P_2(\cos\theta)$ and $V\to0$ at infinity. Find $V(r,\theta)$ and the outward radial field at $r=a^+$. If the interior conductor field is zero, give the outer surface charge density. Check that its total charge vanishes.
permittedResults: A decaying exterior $l$ mode scales as $r^{-(l+1)}P_l(\cos\theta)$.
problems.strategy: Continue each orthogonal angular mode independently with its decaying radial power, then differentiate and use the zero angular average of nonmonopole modes.
hints: The $l=1$ radial factor is $(a/r)^2$ and the $l=2$ factor is $(a/r)^3$.
$E_r=-\partial_rV$.
Both $P_1$ and $P_2$ integrate to zero over the sphere.
problems.solution:
The unique decaying solution is
$$\boxed{V=V_1\left(\frac ar\right)^2\cos\theta+V_2\left(\frac ar\right)^3P_2(\cos\theta)}.$$
Therefore
$$E_r(a^+,\theta)=\frac1a\left[2V_1\cos\theta+3V_2P_2(\cos\theta)\right],$$
and for a conductor
$$\boxed{\sigma(\theta)=\frac{\epsilon_0}{a}\left[2V_1\cos\theta+3V_2P_2(\cos\theta)\right]}.$$
The surface integral of each displayed angular mode is zero, so $Q=0$. No $l=0$ boundary component was prescribed.
rubricCriteria: Assigns the correct decaying radial power to each Legendre mode.
Differentiates to the surface field and applies the conductor jump law.
Uses angular orthogonality to verify zero total charge.

commonErrors.description: Uses growing powers $r^l$ in the exterior domain.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential fails to decay at infinity.

commonErrors.description: Infers nonzero total charge from locally nonzero surface charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero angular averages of the dipole and quadrupole modes are ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The exterior continuation is $V_1(r/a)\cos\theta+V_2(r/a)^2P_2$. Since the surface charge is not identically zero, its integral and the total charge must be positive.

problems.title: Recognize real spherical harmonics from Cartesian coordinates
problems.objective: Solve an interior spherical Dirichlet problem whose boundary data consists of one dipole mode and one quadrupole mode.
problems.statement:
Inside $r<a$, the boundary voltage is
$$V(a,\theta,\phi)=A\sin\theta\cos\phi+B\sin^2\theta\cos2\phi.$$
Use regular solid harmonics, or the Cartesian identities $r\sin\theta\cos\phi=x$ and $r^2\sin^2\theta\cos2\phi=x^2-y^2$, to find $V$ inside. Verify $\nabla^2V=0$, compute $\mathbf E$ at the center, and identify which term affects that center field.
permittedResults: Regular interior modes scale as $r^l$.
$x$ and $x^2-y^2$ are harmonic polynomials.
problems.strategy: Translate each boundary angular factor into its regular Cartesian harmonic, insert the powers of $a$ needed for boundary normalization, and differentiate at the origin.
hints: The first term is $l=1$ and the second is $l=2$.
Try $Ax/a+B(x^2-y^2)/a^2$.
Quadratic terms have zero gradient at the origin.
problems.solution:
The regular continuation is
$$\boxed{V(x,y,z)=\frac Aax+\frac B{a^2}(x^2-y^2)}.$$
At $r=a$ it becomes the prescribed angular function. Also $\nabla^2x=0$ and $\nabla^2(x^2-y^2)=2-2=0$. The field is
$$\mathbf E=-\left(\frac Aa+\frac{2Bx}{a^2},-\frac{2By}{a^2},0\right),$$
so
$$\boxed{\mathbf E(0)=-\frac Aa\hat x}.$$
Only the dipole mode has a nonzero gradient at the center; the quadrupole changes spatial gradients away from it.
rubricCriteria: Matches both boundary factors to regular harmonic polynomials with correct powers of $a$.
Verifies harmonicity explicitly.
Computes the center field and correctly isolates the dipole contribution.

commonErrors.description: Uses inverse powers $r^{-l-1}$ for the interior sphere.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential is singular at the center.

commonErrors.description: Claims the quadrupole contributes a constant field at the center.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero gradient of its quadratic harmonic is overlooked.

problems.flawedProof: Interior modes must decay toward the center, so use $a^2/r^2$ and $a^3/r^3$. The quadrupole has nonzero voltage and therefore adds a uniform center field of magnitude $B/a$.

problems.title: Derive the Fourier-Bessel weight before projecting a constant
problems.objective: Prove orthogonality of radial Dirichlet modes from their Sturm-Liouville equations and compute a concrete expansion coefficient.
problems.statement:
Let $\alpha_n=j_{0n}$ be the positive zeros of $J_0$ and $R_n(s)=J_0(\alpha_ns/a)$ on $0<s<a$. Starting from
$$\frac d{ds}\left(sR_n'\right)+\frac{\alpha_n^2}{a^2}sR_n=0,$$
prove $\int_0^a sR_mR_n\,ds=0$ for $m\ne n$. You may use
$$\int_0^a sR_n^2\,ds=\frac{a^2}{2}J_1(\alpha_n)^2,\qquad \int_0^a sJ_0(\alpha_ns/a)\,ds=\frac{a^2J_1(\alpha_n)}{\alpha_n}.$$
Find the coefficient of $R_n$ in the weighted expansion of $f(s)=1$ and explain why endpoint convergence at $s=a$ need not equal one.
permittedResults: The radial equation, norm, and one required integral are supplied.
problems.strategy: Multiply the two radial equations crosswise, subtract, integrate the total derivative, and only then use the supplied norm for projection.
hints: The eigenvalue difference multiplies $\int sR_mR_n$.
At $s=a$, both $R_m$ and $R_n$ vanish; at the axis the factor $s$ kills the regular boundary term.
Divide the constant's weighted inner product by the supplied squared norm.
problems.solution:
Multiplying the $n$ equation by $R_m$, the $m$ equation by $R_n$, and subtracting gives
$$\frac d{ds}[s(R_mR_n'-R_nR_m')]+\frac{\alpha_n^2-\alpha_m^2}{a^2}sR_mR_n=0.$$
The bracket vanishes at $a$ because both modes are zero and at $0$ by regularity and the factor $s$. Since the eigenvalues differ,
$$\boxed{\int_0^a sR_mR_n\,ds=0}.$$
The constant-function coefficient is
$$c_n=\frac{a^2J_1(\alpha_n)/\alpha_n}{(a^2/2)J_1(\alpha_n)^2} =\boxed{\frac{2}{\alpha_nJ_1(\alpha_n)}}.$$
Every partial sum and each basis function vanishes at $s=a$, so the Dirichlet-series endpoint value is zero rather than the incompatible prescribed value one; the expansion represents the interior limit in the appropriate weighted sense.
rubricCriteria: Derives the Lagrange boundary form and uses both endpoints correctly.
Identifies the cylindrical weight $s$ and proves orthogonality for distinct zeros.
Computes $c_n$ from the supplied integral and norm and addresses endpoint compatibility.

commonErrors.description: Uses unweighted orthogonality $\int R_mR_n ds=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial operator is no longer self-adjoint under the claimed inner product.

commonErrors.description: Claims the series equals one at $s=a$ term by term.
commonErrors.consequence: The Dirichlet basis's zero endpoint is contradicted.

problems.flawedProof: Bessel functions of different zeros are orthogonal under ordinary $ds$, so $c_n=\int_0^aR_n ds$. Because the target is one, the series must also sum to one at the grounded endpoint $s=a$.

problems.title: Project a quartic spherical voltage through quadrupole order
problems.objective: Decompose axisymmetric boundary data into Legendre modes and quantify the exact mean-square remainder after truncation.
problems.statement:
On a sphere, $V(a,\theta)=V_0\cos^4\theta$. Use
$$x^4=\frac15P_0(x)+\frac47P_2(x)+\frac8{35}P_4(x),\qquad \frac12\int_{-1}^1P_l(x)^2dx=\frac1{2l+1}.$$
Find the regular interior potential exactly. Then retain only $l\le2$ and compute the boundary mean-square remainder
$$\frac1{4\pi}\int|V-V_{\le2}|^2d\Omega.$$
Which derivatives of the omitted term can affect the electric field at the center?
permittedResults: The quartic Legendre decomposition and norm are supplied.
problems.strategy: Continue each boundary mode with $(r/a)^l$, then use orthogonality to evaluate the norm of the single omitted $l=4$ component.
hints: Regular interior modes use positive powers of $r$.
The remainder is $(8V_0/35)(r/a)^4P_4$.
A degree-four harmonic has zero gradient at the origin.
problems.solution:
The exact regular solution is
$$\boxed{V=V_0\left[\frac15+\frac47\left(\frac ra\right)^2P_2(\cos\theta) +\frac8{35}\left(\frac ra\right)^4P_4(\cos\theta)\right]}.$$
The $l\le2$ truncation drops only the last term. On the boundary its mean-square remainder is
$$\left(\frac{8V_0}{35}\right)^2\frac1{9} =\boxed{\frac{64V_0^2}{11025}}.$$
The omitted regular solid harmonic begins at degree four, so its value derivatives through third order have the corresponding polynomial behavior; in particular its first derivative vanishes at the origin and it does not alter the center electric field.
rubricCriteria: Continues every Legendre component with the correct regular radial power.
Uses the supplied $P_4$ norm to compute the exact mean-square remainder.
Correctly relates polynomial degree to the center field.

commonErrors.description: Uses exterior powers $(a/r)^{l+1}$ inside the sphere.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential becomes singular at the center.

commonErrors.description: Adds the three mode amplitudes before squaring the truncation error.
commonErrors.consequence: Orthogonality and the fact that only $l=4$ was omitted are lost.

problems.flawedProof: The interior continuation must decay as $(a/r)^{l+1}$. The remainder includes all three coefficients, so its mean square is the square of $1/5+4/7+8/35$.

problems.title: Four charges enforce a grounded right-angle wedge
problems.objective: Construct the image system for two perpendicular grounded planes and derive the force on a charge at an unequal pair of distances.
problems.statement: The grounded planes $x=0$ and $y=0$ bound the region $x>0,y>0$. A point charge $q$ is at $(a,b,0)$ with $a,b>0$. Construct the three image charges, verify zero potential on both planes, and find the force components on $q$. State the behavior when $a\ll b$ and why the line $x=y=0$ is excluded from a smooth-boundary argument.
permittedResults: The physical force equals the force from image charges evaluated at the real charge.
problems.strategy: Reflect across each plane with a sign flip, include the double reflection with its restored sign, then sum the two axial attractions and diagonal repulsion vectorially.
hints: Images are $-q$ at $(-a,b)$ and $(a,-b)$ and $+q$ at $(-a,-b)$.
The single-reflection separations are $2a$ and $2b$.
The double-reflection displacement toward the real charge is $(2a,2b,0)$.
problems.solution:
The stated three images pairwise cancel the real charge on each grounded plane. With $k_e=1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)$, the force is
$$\boxed{F_x=-\frac{k_eq^2}{4a^2}+\frac{k_eq^2a}{4(a^2+b^2)^{3/2}}},$$
$$\boxed{F_y=-\frac{k_eq^2}{4b^2}+\frac{k_eq^2b}{4(a^2+b^2)^{3/2}}},\qquad F_z=0.$$
The first two terms are attractions to the separately reflected charges; the positive-image term points away from $(-a,-b)$. If $a\ll b$, $F_x\sim-k_eq^2/(4a^2)$, the single-plane result near $x=0$. The wedge edge is not a smooth surface point and has enhanced field singular behavior, so smooth local surface formulas must not be applied there without an edge analysis.
rubricCriteria: Builds the complete three-image system with correct signs.
Sums all image forces with correct separations and vector directions.
Checks the near-plane limit and notes the wedge-edge scope.

commonErrors.description: Assigns negative sign to the double-reflected image.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential fails to vanish on one or both grounded planes.

commonErrors.description: Treats all image forces as independently normal to a plane and omits the diagonal components.
commonErrors.consequence: The double-reflection force is not resolved correctly.

problems.flawedProof: Every reflection reverses the charge, so all three images are $-q$. Each plane then pulls only normally, giving $F_x=-k_eq^2/(4a^2)$ and $F_y=-k_eq^2/(4b^2)$ with no diagonal correction.

problems.title: An eight-sign construction grounds the walls of an octant
problems.objective: Generalize repeated reflections to three perpendicular grounded planes and express the image energy without losing the one-half factor.
problems.statement: The planes $x=0,y=0,z=0$ bound the grounded octant $x,y,z>0$. A charge $q$ is at $(a,b,c)$. Construct the seven images using sign triples $(\eta_x,\eta_y,\eta_z)\in\{\pm1\}^3$ and state each image charge. Prove the potential vanishes on every plane. Write a finite exact sum for the interaction energy and force, and evaluate the contribution of the image at $(-a,b,c)$.
permittedResults: For grounded images, the physical energy is one-half the real charge times the image potential at its position.
problems.strategy: Assign a sign $q\eta_x\eta_y\eta_z$ to each reflected position, omit the all-positive real charge, and pair sign triples to prove cancellation on a wall.
hints: One reflection changes sign; two restore it; three change it again.
At $x=0$, pair terms with opposite $\eta_x$.
Differentiate the image potential only after writing the finite sum.
problems.solution:
Place
$$q_{\boldsymbol\eta}=q\eta_x\eta_y\eta_z \quad\hbox{at}\quad(\eta_xa,\eta_yb,\eta_zc)$$
for all sign triples except $(+,+,+)$. On $x=0$, terms differing only in $\eta_x$ have equal distance and opposite charge; similarly for the other planes. Hence all three walls are grounded. If $\mathbf r_0=(a,b,c)$,
$$\boxed{U=\frac{k_eq^2}{2}\sum_{\boldsymbol\eta\ne(+,+,+)} \frac{\eta_x\eta_y\eta_z}{|\mathbf r_0-(\eta_xa,\eta_yb,\eta_zc)|}},$$
and
$$\boxed{\mathbf F=k_eq^2\sum_{\boldsymbol\eta\ne(+,+,+)} \eta_x\eta_y\eta_z\frac{\mathbf r_0-\mathbf r_{\boldsymbol\eta}}{|\mathbf r_0-\mathbf r_{\boldsymbol\eta}|^3}}.$$
The image at $(-a,b,c)$ has charge $-q$, contributes $-k_eq^2/(4a)$ to $U$, including the physical one-half, and contributes $-k_eq^2\hat x/(4a^2)$ to the force.
rubricCriteria: Assigns image signs by reflection parity and omits only the real charge.
Proves cancellation on each plane by pairing sign triples.
Writes correct energy and force sums and evaluates the requested image contribution.

commonErrors.description: Uses charge $-q$ for all seven images.
commonErrors.consequence: Double-reflection pairs no longer cancel the potential on every plane.

commonErrors.description: Uses $U=qV_{\rm image}$ without one-half.
commonErrors.consequence: The work of building induced charge is double-counted.

problems.flawedProof: All walls are grounded if every reflected charge is negative. The energy is simply $q$ times the image potential, so the nearest image contributes $-k_eq^2/(2a)$.

problems.title: An infinite image ladder fits between two grounded plates
problems.objective: Verify the image-series potential between parallel grounded planes and extract its nearest-wall force asymptotics.
problems.statement:
Grounded plates lie at $z=0$ and $z=L$. A charge $q$ is at $(0,0,a)$, $0<a<L$. Consider
$$V(\rho,z)=k_eq\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\left[ \frac1{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z-a-2nL)^2}}- \frac1{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z+a-2nL)^2}}\right].$$
Verify both boundary values by reindexing, explain convergence away from the source, and find the two nearest-image contributions to $F_z$. Give the leading limit when $a\ll L$.
permittedResults: Terms may be paired symmetrically in $n$ when discussing convergence.
problems.strategy: Use termwise cancellation at the lower plate and an integer shift at the upper plate, pair remote images to expose their faster decay, then isolate the nearest image behind each wall.
hints: At $z=0$, the two denominators match after $n\mapsto-n$.
At $z=L$, use $n\mapsto1-n$.
The nearest lower image is $-q$ at $-a$; the nearest upper image is $-q$ at $2L-a$.
problems.solution:
At $z=0$, the positive and negative ladders cancel after $n\mapsto-n$. At $z=L$, they cancel after $n\mapsto1-n$, so both plates are grounded. Symmetric pairing cancels the $1/|n|$ tails, leaving a convergent $O(n^{-2})$ potential series away from the real source. The lower image gives
$$F_z^{(0)}=-\frac{k_eq^2}{4a^2},$$
and the nearest upper image gives
$$F_z^{(L)}=+\frac{k_eq^2}{4(L-a)^2}.$$
All other images give finite smaller corrections. Thus for $a\ll L$,
$$\boxed{F_z=-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0a^2}+O(q^2/(\epsilon_0L^2))},$$
directed toward the nearby lower plate.
rubricCriteria: Verifies both grounded plates with the correct reindexings.
Explains convergence through symmetric cancellation rather than absolute $1/n$ convergence.
Computes the two nearest-image force terms and the near-wall asymptotic.

commonErrors.description: Checks only the $z=0$ boundary and assumes the upper plate follows.
commonErrors.consequence: The essential second ladder reindexing is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Uses distance $a$ rather than $2a$ to the lower image.
commonErrors.consequence: The leading force is four times too large.

problems.flawedProof: Every summand vanishes separately at both plates, so no reindexing is needed. The lower image is distance $a$ away and gives $-k_eq^2/a^2$.

problems.title: Invert a line charge across a grounded cylinder
problems.objective: Use the two-dimensional image construction to ground a conducting cylinder and compute force per unit length with a controlled reference constant.
problems.statement: An infinite line charge $\lambda$ runs parallel to the axis of a grounded conducting cylinder of radius $a$. In cross-section the line is at $s=d>a$. Show that an image line $-\lambda$ at $s'=a^2/d$ makes the cylinder an equipotential, choose the additive constant that makes it zero, and find the force per unit length on the real line. Check $d\downarrow a$ and $d\gg a$.
permittedResults: A line charge has potential $-(\lambda/2\pi\epsilon_0)\ln(R/R_0)$.
problems.strategy: Use the inversion-distance ratio on the circle to prove it is constant, set that constant to zero, and obtain force from the image field at the real line.
hints: For a point on $s=a$, the distance ratio to the real and image lines is $d/a$.
Only a constant is needed after the two logarithms are combined.
The real-image separation is $d-a^2/d$.
problems.solution:
Let $R$ and $R'$ be distances to the real and image lines. On $s=a$, inversion geometry gives $R/R'=d/a$, independent of angle. Therefore
$$V=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln R+\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln R'+\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac da$$
vanishes on the cylinder. The image field attracts the real line, so
$$\boxed{\frac FL=-\frac{\lambda^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0(d-a^2/d)}\hat{\mathbf s}}.$$
As $d=a+h$ with $h\ll a$, the separation is $2h+O(h^2/a)$ and $F/L\sim-\lambda^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0h)$, the grounded-plane line-charge limit. For $d\gg a$, $F/L\sim-\lambda^2/(2\pi\epsilon_0d)$.
rubricCriteria: Uses the inversion location and constant distance ratio to ground the circle.
Handles the logarithmic additive reference explicitly.
Computes the image force per length and both geometric limits.

commonErrors.description: Places the image at $a^2/d$ with the same sign as the real line.
commonErrors.consequence: The cylinder is not an equipotential at zero.

commonErrors.description: Uses the center distance $d$ instead of the real-image separation.
commonErrors.consequence: The force and near-wall limit are wrong.

problems.flawedProof: The image has charge $+\lambda$ because inversion preserves source sign. Its distance from the real line is $d$, so the force is repulsive $+\lambda^2/(2\pi\epsilon_0d)$.

problems.title: Fix the sign in the Dirichlet Green representation
problems.objective: Derive the electrostatic Green-function formula from Green's identity and verify its volume-source term in a grounded half-space.
problems.statement:
Let $\nabla'^2G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')$ and $G=0$ on a boundary. Derive the formula for $V$ satisfying $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0$ with prescribed boundary value $f$. State the sign of the outward-normal derivative term. For the grounded upper half-space, verify
$$G=\frac1{4\pi}\left(\frac1{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}-\frac1{|\mathbf r-\bar{\mathbf r}'|}\right)$$
and use it for one point charge.
permittedResults: Use Green's second identity in the source coordinate $\mathbf r'$.
problems.strategy: Keep the convention $\nabla^2G=-\delta$ fixed through the identity, solve algebraically for $V(\mathbf r)$, and then recognize the half-space expression as a real charge minus its mirror.
hints: Green's identity contains $V\partial_nG-G\partial_nV$.
The delta term contributes $-V(\mathbf r)$.
The reflected point has the opposite sign and lies below the plane.
problems.solution:
Green's second identity yields
$$-V(\mathbf r)+\frac1{\epsilon_0}\int_\Omega G\rho\,d\tau' =\oint_{\partial\Omega}f\,\partial_{n'}G\,da'.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{V(\mathbf r)=\frac1{\epsilon_0}\int G\rho\,d\tau'- \oint f\,\partial_{n'}G\,da'}.$$
The boundary term has a minus sign for the stated $G$ convention and outward normal. In the upper half-space, the two Coulomb kernels have coincident values on the plane, so $G=0$, and only the first has its delta source inside. For $\rho=q\delta(\mathbf r'-\mathbf r_0')$ and $f=0$,
$$V=\frac q{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac1{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0'|}-\frac1{|\mathbf r-\bar{\mathbf r}_0'|}\right),$$
the standard grounded-plane image potential.
rubricCriteria: Derives the representation with a consistent Green-function convention.
Gets the outward-normal boundary-term sign correct.
Verifies the half-space boundary and applies the volume term to a point source.

commonErrors.description: Uses the representation for $\nabla^2G=+\delta$ while declaring $\nabla^2G=-\delta$.
commonErrors.consequence: Both source and boundary signs become inconsistent.

commonErrors.description: Places the half-space image with the same sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The Green function does not vanish on the grounded plane.

problems.flawedProof: Because $\nabla^2G=-\delta$, the source term enters with a minus sign and the boundary term with a plus sign. The half-space image must have the same sign so its potential reinforces the real source on the plane.

problems.title: Reciprocity turns a weighting potential into induced charge
problems.objective: Derive Green reciprocity for conductor configurations and use a unit-voltage auxiliary problem to compute an electrode's induced charge.
problems.statement:
Two electrostatic configurations share the same linear dielectric region and conductor geometry. Derive
$$\int\rho_1V_2d\tau+\sum_iQ_i^{(1)}V_i^{(2)} =\int\rho_2V_1d\tau+\sum_iQ_i^{(2)}V_i^{(1)}.$$
In the actual configuration, all conductors are grounded and a point charge $q$ is at $\mathbf r_0$. In an auxiliary configuration there is no volume charge, electrode $A$ is at unit potential, and all other electrodes are grounded. If its potential is $w_A(\mathbf r)$, find the actual induced charge $Q_A$.
permittedResults: Surface charge integrates to each conductor charge $Q_i$.
problems.strategy: Apply Green's second identity to the two potentials, convert conductor surface integrals into constant voltage times total charge, then specialize every zero voltage and zero density carefully.
hints: The volume cross terms are symmetric after using Poisson's equation.
In the actual state, $V_i^{(1)}=0$.
In the auxiliary state, only $V_A^{(2)}=1$.
problems.solution:
Green's identity and $\partial_nV=-\sigma/\epsilon$ on the dielectric side convert the boundary terms into the displayed conductor sums, giving reciprocity. Choose configuration 1 as actual and 2 as auxiliary. Then
$$\int\rho_1V_2d\tau=q\,w_A(\mathbf r_0),$$
and the only nonzero conductor-voltage term on the left is $Q_A^{(1)}$. The right side vanishes because $\rho_2=0$ and every actual conductor potential is zero. Therefore
$$\boxed{Q_A=-q\,w_A(\mathbf r_0)}.$$
The minus sign reflects the grounded electrode charge induced by a positive interior source; $0\le w_A\le1$ in ordinary connected geometries by the maximum principle.
rubricCriteria: Derives reciprocity with both volume and conductor terms.
Specializes the actual and auxiliary configurations without dropping the actual electrode charge.
Obtains the weighting-potential formula with the correct sign.

commonErrors.description: Sets the conductor charge term to zero because the conductor voltage is zero in the actual state.
commonErrors.consequence: The cross-configuration voltage factor is overlooked and the desired induced charge disappears.

commonErrors.description: Reports $Q_A=+qw_A$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reciprocity balance and grounded-screening sign are reversed.

problems.flawedProof: Grounded conductors have zero voltage, so every conductor term vanishes in both configurations. Reciprocity then gives $qw_A=0$, or alternatively $Q_A=+qw_A$ if one inserts the charge by hand.

problems.title: Read physics from the Maxwell capacitance matrix
problems.objective: Derive symmetry, gauge nullspace, sign structure, and energy positivity for a complete conductor capacitance matrix.
problems.statement:
Let $N$ conductor boundary components enclose a connected dielectric region, and include the enclosing reference conductor in the list rather than silently fixing it as ground. No conductor potential is fixed a priori. Define $Q_i=\sum_jC_{ij}V_j$. Use reciprocity to prove $C_{ij}=C_{ji}$. Use invariance under the simultaneous shift $V_j\mapsto V_j+V_0$ to derive the row sums. Explain why $C_{ii}>0$ and $C_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and show
$$U=\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V\ge0.$$
Why is this complete all-boundary matrix singular, and how does choosing one conductor as the voltage reference produce a nonsingular reduced matrix?
permittedResults: The electrostatic field energy is nonnegative and reciprocity is available.
problems.strategy: Excite one conductor at a time for reciprocity and signs, use the included reference conductor to make a common potential shift a genuine gauge transformation, and identify the quadratic energy with field energy.
hints: A unit excitation of conductor $j$ defines column $j$.
A common voltage produces no electric field and no charge.
Off-diagonal charge induced on grounded conductors opposes the excited conductor.
problems.solution:
Applying reciprocity to unit-voltage excitations of conductors $i$ and $j$ gives $C_{ij}=C_{ji}$. Because the enclosing reference conductor is included and no external potential has been fixed, a common shift of every listed conductor potential produces no electric field and no charge. Hence
$$\boxed{\sum_jC_{ij}=0},$$
and $C\mathbf1=0$. With only conductor $i$ positive relative to all the others, it carries positive charge, so $C_{ii}>0$, while the other grounded conductors acquire nonpositive induced charges, so $C_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$. Finally,
$$\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V=\frac12\sum_iQ_iV_i=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int|\mathbf E|^2d\tau\ge0.$$
The common-voltage vector is a null vector, making the complete all-boundary matrix singular. Fixing one conductor voltage and deleting its row and column removes that gauge degree and yields the usual positive-definite reduced matrix for a connected finite geometry. By contrast, a matrix listing only finite conductors while holding spatial infinity at zero is already reference-fixed; it is generally nonsingular and its row sums need not vanish.
rubricCriteria: Uses reciprocity to establish matrix symmetry.
Derives the zero row sums and common-voltage nullspace using the explicitly included reference conductor, and obtains the physical entry signs from controlled excitations.
Connects the quadratic form to field energy and explains reference reduction.

commonErrors.description: Claims every row sums to a positive self-capacitance.
commonErrors.consequence: Gauge invariance under common voltage shifts is violated.

commonErrors.description: Calls the complete matrix positive definite.
commonErrors.consequence: Its unavoidable common-voltage null vector is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Each diagonal entry is a capacitance, so every row sum is positive and the full matrix is positive definite. Off-diagonal entries must also be positive because raising any voltage increases all charges.

problems.title: Assemble a three-shell capacitance matrix from two gaps
problems.objective: Compute conductor charges and energy for three concentric spherical shells by treating adjacent dielectric gaps as coupled capacitors.
problems.statement:
Three thin concentric conducting shells have radii $a<b<c$ and potentials $V_a,V_b,V_c$. Assume zero exterior field outside $c$. Define
$$C_1=4\pi\epsilon_0\frac{ab}{b-a},\qquad C_2=4\pi\epsilon_0\frac{bc}{c-b}.$$
Derive $Q_a,Q_b,Q_c$, write the full $3\times3$ capacitance matrix, and verify symmetry, row sums, total charge, and energy. Evaluate the charges when $(V_a,V_b,V_c)=(V_0,0,0)$.
permittedResults: The two adjacent-gap capacitances are supplied.
problems.strategy: Write each gap charge as capacitance times its voltage difference, assign equal opposite charges to its two faces, then sum the two contributions on the middle shell.
hints: The middle shell receives one contribution from each gap.
Zero exterior field makes the three total charges sum to zero.
problems.solution:
The charges are
$$\boxed{Q_a=C_1(V_a-V_b)},$$
$$\boxed{Q_b=C_1(V_b-V_a)+C_2(V_b-V_c)},$$
$$\boxed{Q_c=C_2(V_c-V_b)}.$$
Thus
$$C=\begin{pmatrix}C_1&-C_1&0\\-C_1&C_1+C_2&-C_2\\0&-C_2&C_2\end{pmatrix}.$$
It is symmetric, each row sums to zero, and $Q_a+Q_b+Q_c=0$. The energy is
$$U=\frac12C_1(V_a-V_b)^2+\frac12C_2(V_b-V_c)^2.$$
For $(V_0,0,0)$, $(Q_a,Q_b,Q_c)=(C_1V_0,-C_1V_0,0)$.
rubricCriteria: Assigns equal-opposite gap charges and sums the middle-shell contributions.
Builds the exact symmetric matrix and verifies its row sums and total charge.
Obtains the voltage-difference energy and requested excitation charges.

commonErrors.description: Sets $Q_b=C_2(V_b-V_c)$ and omits the inner-gap face.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge conservation and the matrix middle diagonal fail.

commonErrors.description: Writes energy using absolute potentials rather than gap differences.
commonErrors.consequence: A common voltage shift incorrectly changes the energy.

problems.flawedProof: Each shell has only its outward-facing capacitance, so $Q_b=C_2(V_b-V_c)$. The energy is $(C_1V_a^2+C_2V_b^2)/2$, which depends on the chosen zero of potential.

problems.title: A linear coaxial trial potential bounds the capacitance from above
problems.objective: Apply the Dirichlet principle to a nonharmonic trial function and interpret the resulting fixed-voltage energy bound correctly.
problems.statement:
A coaxial capacitor has radii $a<b$, length $L$, and fixed boundary values $V(a)=V_0$, $V(b)=0$. The exact capacitance per length is $C/L=2\pi\epsilon_0/\ln(b/a)$. Use the admissible trial potential
$$V_t(s)=V_0\frac{b-s}{b-a}$$
to compute $U_t/L=(\epsilon_0/2)\int_a^b|V_t'|^2\,2\pi s\,ds$. By the Dirichlet principle, the harmonic solution minimizes this fixed-boundary energy. Derive the resulting capacitance bound and verify it for $b=2a$.
permittedResults: At fixed voltage, $U=(1/2)CV^2$.
The exact capacitance is supplied for comparison.
problems.strategy: Compute the trial gradient and cylindrical measure exactly, translate the energy inequality at fixed voltage into a capacitance inequality, and check its direction numerically.
hints: Integrate $s$ from $a$ to $b$.
A larger trial energy at the same $V_0$ means a larger trial capacitance estimate.
problems.solution:
The trial energy is
$$\frac{U_t}{L}=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{(b-a)^2}2\pi\int_a^b s\,ds =\frac{\pi\epsilon_0V_0^2(b+a)}{2(b-a)}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\frac{C}{L}\le\frac{C_t}{L}=\frac{2U_t/L}{V_0^2} =\pi\epsilon_0\frac{b+a}{b-a}}.$$
For $b=2a$, the trial bound is $3\pi\epsilon_0$, while the exact value is $2\pi\epsilon_0/\ln2\approx2.885\pi\epsilon_0$, so the direction is correct. The bound is on capacitance because voltage, not charge, is fixed.
rubricCriteria: Evaluates the trial field energy with the cylindrical measure.
Converts the minimizing-energy statement into the correct fixed-voltage capacitance bound.
Checks the inequality numerically at $b=2a$.

commonErrors.description: Interprets minimum fixed-voltage energy as an upper bound on the exact energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The capacitance inequality is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses planar measure $ds$ instead of $2\pi s\,ds$.
commonErrors.consequence: The estimate has wrong geometry and dimensions.

problems.flawedProof: The exact solution maximizes energy, so $C\ge C_t$. Using a planar integral gives $C_t/L=\epsilon_0/(b-a)$, which is the required cylindrical upper bound.

problems.title: Flatten a weakly corrugated grounded conductor to first order
problems.objective: Derive the leading potential and surface-charge modulation caused by a small sinusoidal boundary displacement.
problems.statement: Vacuum lies above a grounded conductor whose surface is $z=\varepsilon\cos(kx)$, with $|\varepsilon k|\ll1$. Far above it, $V\sim E_0z$. Write $V=E_0z+\varepsilon V_1+O(\varepsilon^2)$, expand the boundary condition about $z=0$, and find the decaying $V_1$. Compute the conductor surface charge through first order, using the normal from conductor into vacuum, and show its spatial mean is unchanged.
permittedResults: A decaying harmonic with boundary cosine is proportional to $e^{-kz}\cos(kx)$.
problems.strategy: Taylor-expand the zero-potential condition on the displaced surface, solve the resulting flat-boundary harmonic problem, and keep only first-order terms when evaluating the normal field.
hints: At first order, $0=E_0\varepsilon\cos(kx)+\varepsilon V_1(x,0)$.
Choose the solution that decays as $z\to\infty$.
Slope corrections multiply a tangential field already of first order and do not affect $\sigma$ at this order.
problems.solution:
The expanded boundary condition gives $V_1(x,0)=-E_0\cos(kx)$, so
$$\boxed{V=E_0z-\varepsilon E_0e^{-kz}\cos(kx)+O(\varepsilon^2)}.$$
To first order the outward conductor normal is effectively $+\hat z$ for the normal-field calculation, and
$$E_z=-\partial_zV=-E_0-\varepsilon E_0k e^{-kz}\cos(kx).$$
At the surface,
$$\boxed{\sigma(x)=\epsilon_0E_n=-\epsilon_0E_0[1+\varepsilon k\cos(kx)]+O(\varepsilon^2)}.$$
The cosine averages to zero, so the mean remains $-\epsilon_0E_0$. Negative charge is enhanced where the conductor protrudes into the field.
rubricCriteria: Linearizes the boundary condition at the correct reference plane.
Finds the unique decaying first-order harmonic correction.
Computes the surface-charge sign and modulation and verifies its unchanged mean.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+E_0e^{-kz}\cos(kx)$ for the correction.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential is nonzero on the displaced conductor at first order.

commonErrors.description: Adds a nonzero mean first-order charge from the cosine corrugation.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero spatial average of the perturbation is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The boundary displacement raises the potential, so add $+\varepsilon E_0e^{-kz}\cos kx$. Every bump increases charge, hence the mean surface charge also increases at first order.

problems.title: Mixed boundary data are unique when a Dirichlet piece is present
problems.objective: Extend the energy uniqueness proof to disjoint Dirichlet and Neumann boundary portions and identify the pure-Neumann exception.
problems.statement: Let $\partial\Omega=\Gamma_D\cup\Gamma_N$ with disjoint pieces. Two Poisson solutions have the same $V$ on $\Gamma_D$ and the same $\partial_nV$ on $\Gamma_N$. Prove uniqueness if $\Gamma_D$ contains a nonempty open boundary piece. Explain why the proof leaves an additive constant when $\Gamma_D$ is empty. Apply the result to the rectangle in ED047.
permittedResults: Green's first identity may be used for the harmonic difference.
problems.strategy: Apply the energy identity to the difference and split the boundary integral according to which factor vanishes on each piece.
hints: On $\Gamma_D$, the difference $u$ is zero.
On $\Gamma_N$, its normal derivative is zero.
A constant that vanishes on a nonempty Dirichlet piece is zero.
problems.solution:
The difference $u$ is harmonic. Green's identity gives
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2d\tau=\oint_{\Gamma_D}u\partial_nu\,da+ \oint_{\Gamma_N}u\partial_nu\,da.$$
The first integral vanishes because $u=0$ on $\Gamma_D$ and the second because $\partial_nu=0$ on $\Gamma_N$. Thus $\nabla u=0$, so $u$ is constant. A nonempty Dirichlet piece forces that constant to zero. If $\Gamma_D$ is empty, the constant survives, subject also to Neumann compatibility. In ED047, the three Dirichlet sides form a nonempty set and the bottom is Neumann, so the separated solution is unique.
rubricCriteria: Forms the harmonic difference and partitions the boundary term correctly.
Uses the appropriate vanishing factor on each boundary piece.
Distinguishes mixed uniqueness from the pure-Neumann constant and applies it to ED047.

commonErrors.description: Requires both $u=0$ and $\partial_nu=0$ on every boundary piece.
commonErrors.consequence: The mixed proof is incorrectly declared impossible.

commonErrors.description: Claims a nonempty Neumann piece fixes the additive constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Normal derivatives are unchanged by constants.

problems.flawedProof: Mixed data cannot give uniqueness because neither factor in $u\partial_nu$ vanishes on the entire boundary. Any Neumann segment nevertheless fixes the constant because it specifies a derivative.

problems.title: A logarithmic conformal coordinate straightens a conducting wedge
problems.objective: Solve the two-dimensional potential between wedge faces and track the corner field and electrode charge per logarithmic length.
problems.statement: In a two-dimensional wedge $0<\phi<\alpha$, the face $\phi=0$ is at $0$ and the face $\phi=\alpha$ at $V_0$. Use the conformal coordinate $w=\log z=\ln r+i\phi$, which maps the wedge to a strip, to find $V$. Compute $\mathbf E$, the charge density on each face, and the charge per unit out-of-plane length carried between radii $r_1$ and $r_2$. Explain the $r\to0$ singularity and the scale invariance.
permittedResults: The imaginary part of an analytic coordinate is harmonic.
problems.strategy: Recognize that the strip solution is linear in its transverse coordinate $\phi$, then convert its gradient back with the cylindrical $1/r$ metric factor.
hints: In the strip, $V=V_0\operatorname{Im}w/\alpha$.
The field is $-(1/r)\partial_\phi V\,\hat\phi$.
Integrate the face charge along $dr$.
problems.solution:
The strip solution pulls back to
$$\boxed{V(r,\phi)=\frac{V_0}{\alpha}\phi}.$$
It is harmonic away from the vertex and meets both face voltages. The field is
$$\boxed{\mathbf E=-\frac{V_0}{\alpha r}\hat\phi}.$$
Normals from the lower and upper conductors into the wedge are $+\hat\phi$ and $-\hat\phi$, respectively, so their charges are $-\epsilon_0V_0/(\alpha r)$ and $+\epsilon_0V_0/(\alpha r)$. The magnitude of charge per out-of-plane length between $r_1$ and $r_2$ is
$$\boxed{|Q'|=\frac{\epsilon_0|V_0|}{\alpha}\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}}.$$
The $1/r$ corner field is singular, while scaling both radii leaves their ratio and hence the dimensionless geometry unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Uses the logarithmic map to obtain the linear strip potential.
Computes the metric-correct field and both face-charge signs.
Integrates the logarithmic charge and interprets corner singularity and scale invariance.

commonErrors.description: Uses $E_\phi=-\partial_\phi V$ without the cylindrical $1/r$ factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The field has wrong units and misses the corner singularity.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the same surface-charge sign to both wedge faces.
commonErrors.consequence: The opposing conductor normals and capacitor charge balance are ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The strip voltage is linear in $r$, so $V=V_0r/\alpha$ and the field is uniform. Both faces see the same normal direction and therefore carry equal charges of the same sign.

problems.title: Perturb the field of a nearly spherical conductor without moving its voltage
problems.objective: Linearize a deformed equipotential boundary, solve the induced multipole problem, and distinguish local charge modulation from total capacitance change.
problems.statement:
A conductor held at fixed voltage $V_0$ has surface
$$r_s(\theta)=a[1+\eta P_2(\cos\theta)],\qquad |\eta|\ll1,$$
and $V\to0$ at infinity. Starting from the spherical solution $V^{(0)}=V_0a/r$, write $V=V^{(0)}+\eta V^{(1)}+O(\eta^2)$. Taylor-expand the boundary condition at $r=a$ to determine $V^{(1)}$, then find the exterior potential and surface charge density through first order. Finally integrate the charge over the deformed surface and decide whether the capacitance changes at order $\eta$.

Use the normal from the conductor into vacuum and retain all first-order effects from evaluating the field and area at $r=r_s$.
permittedResults: The decaying axisymmetric exterior harmonic of degree $l$ is proportional to $r^{-l-1}P_l(\cos\theta)$.
$\int P_2(\cos\theta)d\Omega=0$.
problems.strategy: Expand the fixed-potential condition on the reference sphere, continue the resulting quadrupole boundary value outward, and separately expand the radial field and surface measure.
hints: The displaced-surface condition gives $V^{(1)}(a)=-aP_2\,\partial_rV^{(0)}(a)$.
The normal-tilt correction multiplies a zeroth-order tangential field that vanishes.
To first order, $da=a^2[1+2\eta P_2]d\Omega$.
problems.solution:
Expanding $V(r_s,\theta)=V_0$ gives
$$V^{(1)}(a,\theta)+aP_2\partial_r\left(\frac{V_0a}{r}\right)_{r=a}=0,$$
so $V^{(1)}(a,\theta)=V_0P_2(\cos\theta)$. The unique decaying continuation is therefore
$$\boxed{V=V_0\left[\frac ar+\eta\left(\frac ar\right)^3P_2(\cos\theta)\right]+O(\eta^2)}.$$
The zeroth-order field has no tangential component, so tilting the normal contributes only at second order. Evaluating $E_r=-\partial_rV$ at $r=a(1+\eta P_2)$ gives
$$E_n=\frac{V_0}{a}[1-2\eta P_2+3\eta P_2]+O(\eta^2) =\frac{V_0}{a}[1+\eta P_2]+O(\eta^2).$$
Hence
$$\boxed{\sigma(\theta)=\frac{\epsilon_0V_0}{a}[1+\eta P_2(\cos\theta)]+O(\eta^2)}.$$
Using $da=a^2(1+2\eta P_2)d\Omega$ and the zero angular mean of $P_2$,
$$Q=\int\sigma da=4\pi\epsilon_0aV_0+O(\eta^2).$$
Thus $C=Q/V_0=4\pi\epsilon_0a+O(\eta^2)$: the quadrupolar deformation redistributes charge locally but does not change capacitance at first order.
rubricCriteria: Linearizes the displaced equipotential and obtains the correct exterior quadrupole amplitude.
Expands the normal field at the displaced surface with the correct sign and coefficient.
Includes the area change, integrates the charge, and correctly identifies the absent first-order capacitance shift.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $V^{(1)}(a)=0$ because the conductor voltage is fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The displacement of the zeroth-order potential is omitted and the deformed surface is not equipotential.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the perturbed density using the undeformed area and treats the $P_2$ term as a nonzero mean.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious first-order capacitance change is reported.

problems.flawedProof: Fixed voltage means every perturbative term vanishes at $r=a$, so the old spherical potential remains exact. The bulges have larger area and therefore increase $Q$ linearly, even though no field correction is needed.

problems.title: Trap a finite two-conductor capacitance between dual trial fields
problems.objective: Combine the Dirichlet and Thomson principles into certified upper and lower bounds with consistent units.
problems.statement:
An inner finite conductor is surrounded by a finite grounded outer conductor in a homogeneous dielectric of permittivity $\epsilon$. Let $C$ be their capacitance. A dimensionless trial potential $u_t$ equals $1$ on the inner conductor and $0$ on the outer conductor. A normalized flux field $\mathbf d_t$, with units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, is divergence-free in the dielectric, has zero normal component on any insulating symmetry boundary, and carries dimensionless outward flux $1$ from the inner conductor to the outer.
