Thus $Q\mathbf d_t$ is an admissible physical displacement field for charge $Q$.

Define
$$D_t=\epsilon\int_\Omega|\nabla u_t|^2d\tau,\qquad T_t=\int_\Omega\frac{|\mathbf d_t|^2}{2\epsilon}d\tau.$$
Prove the certified bracket
$$\frac1{2T_t}\le C\le D_t.$$
For a particular geometry, careful trial integrations give $D_t=6.20\epsilon a$ and $T_t=0.0875/(\epsilon a)$. Evaluate the bracket and explain what it would mean if the numerical lower bound exceeded the numerical upper bound.
permittedResults: At fixed boundary voltage, the harmonic potential minimizes $\frac\epsilon2\int|\nabla V|^2$.
At fixed free charge and admissible flux, the electrostatic displacement minimizes $\int|\mathbf D|^2/(2\epsilon)$.
problems.strategy: Normalize the voltage trial to one volt and the flux trial to one coulomb, translate each minimum-energy inequality into a statement about $C$, and only then substitute the trial numbers.
hints: For a one-volt exact solution, $U=C/2$.
For a one-coulomb exact solution, $U=1/(2C)$.
The two trial principles bound reciprocal quantities in opposite directions.
problems.solution:
With a one-volt boundary difference, the trial potential has energy $D_t/2$. Dirichlet minimization gives
$$\frac C2\le\frac{D_t}{2},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad C\le D_t.$$
For general charge $Q$, the normalized trial field has energy $Q^2T_t$, whereas the exact energy is $Q^2/(2C)$. Thomson minimization gives
$$\frac1{2C}\le T_t,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad C\ge\frac1{2T_t}.$$
Together,
$$\boxed{\frac1{2T_t}\le C\le D_t}.$$
The supplied values yield
$$\frac1{2T_t}=\frac{\epsilon a}{0.175}=5.714\ldots\epsilon a,$$
so
$$\boxed{5.71\epsilon a\le C\le6.20\epsilon a}.$$
$D_t$ has units of capacitance, while $T_t$ has units of inverse capacitance because $\mathbf d_t$ is normalized per unit charge. A reversed numerical bracket would not disprove the principles; it would certify an error in a trial field's admissibility, normalization, units, or integration.
rubricCriteria: Applies the fixed-voltage variational principle to obtain the capacitance upper bound.
Applies the unit-charge flux principle to obtain the reciprocal lower bound.
Evaluates the numerical bracket with correct dimensions and diagnoses an inconsistent bracket as a trial calculation failure.

commonErrors.description: Uses both minimum principles as upper bounds on $C$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reciprocal relation between fixed-charge energy and capacitance is lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats $T_t$ as having capacitance units and compares it directly with $D_t$.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerical bracket is dimensionally meaningless.

problems.flawedProof: Both exact fields minimize energy, so $C\le D_t$ and $C\le T_t$. Since $T_t<D_t$ numerically, the best upper bound is $0.0875\epsilon a$ and no lower bound is available.

problems.title: Ground a sphere with a Kelvin image and audit every physical limit
problems.objective: Construct the canonical grounded-sphere image solution, derive induced charge and force, and test planar and far-field limits.
problems.statement:
A grounded conducting sphere of radius $a$ is centered at the origin. A point charge $q$ lies on the positive $z$ axis at $z=d>a$. Construct the Kelvin image charge and its location, prove the resulting exterior potential vanishes on $r=a$, and compute: (i) the total induced charge, (ii) the surface charge density as a function of polar angle, (iii) the physical interaction energy, and (iv) the force on $q$.

Check both $h=d-a\ll a$ and $d\gg a$. In the near-surface limit, compare the force with that from a charge a distance $h$ from a grounded plane. Use $k_e=1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)$.
permittedResults: The physical image energy is one-half $q$ times the image potential at the real charge.
For points on $r=a$, the distances to axial points at $d$ and $a^2/d$ differ by the factor $d/a$.
problems.strategy: Choose the inverted source so the two Coulomb terms cancel pointwise on the sphere, then derive charge, energy, and force from distinct physical rules rather than differentiating a moving image naively.
hints: Try $q'=-qa/d$ at $d'=a^2/d$.
The coefficient of the exterior $1/r$ term gives $q+Q_{\rm ind}$.
Differentiate the physical energy after substituting the $d$-dependent image data, or compute the image force directly.
problems.solution:
The image is
$$\boxed{q'=-\frac{a}{d}q,\qquad d'=\frac{a^2}{d}}.$$
Thus, in the exterior region,
$$V=k_e\left[\frac q{|\mathbf r-d\hat z|}+\frac{q'}{|\mathbf r-d'\hat z|}\right].$$
On $r=a$, the distance ratio is $|\mathbf r-d\hat z|=(d/a)|\mathbf r-d'\hat z|$, so the two terms cancel. At large $r$, the conductor contributes the image monopole; hence
$$\boxed{Q_{\rm ind}=q'=-\frac{qa}{d}}.$$
Normal differentiation on the sphere gives
$$\boxed{\sigma(\theta)=-\frac{q}{4\pi a}\frac{d^2-a^2}{(d^2+a^2-2ad\cos\theta)^{3/2}}}.$$
The physical energy and force are
$$\boxed{U=\frac12k_e\frac{qq'}{d-d'}=-\frac{k_eq^2a}{2(d^2-a^2)}},$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F=-\frac{k_eq^2ad}{(d^2-a^2)^2}\hat z}.$$
For $d=a+h$ with $h\ll a$, $F_z\sim-k_eq^2/(4h^2)=-q^2/(16\pi\epsilon_0h^2)$, the grounded-plane result. For $d\gg a$, $Q_{\rm ind}\sim-qa/d$, $U\sim-k_eq^2a/(2d^2)$, and $F_z\sim-k_eq^2a/d^3$, all vanishing with separation.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the inverted image and verifies the boundary value pointwise.
Derives the induced total and surface charge with correct sign and dimensions.
Uses the one-half factor only in energy, obtains the exact force, and verifies both near-plane and far-field limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses image charge $-q$ at $a^2/d$.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential does not cancel at every point of the spherical boundary and the induced total charge is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Applies the energy one-half factor to the force from the image.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical force is incorrectly smaller by a factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: Reflection across a grounded surface always uses $-q$, so put $-q$ at $a^2/d$. The image force must then be divided by two because the energy has a one-half factor, giving the planar limit $-q^2/(32\pi\epsilon_0h^2)$.

problems.title: Close a rational-angle wedge image group and sum its energy
problems.objective: Build the finite image orbit for a grounded wedge of angle $\pi/N$ and evaluate a nontrivial $N=3$ energy.
problems.statement:
A point charge $q$ lies at cylindrical coordinates $(\rho,\phi_0,z=0)$ inside the grounded wedge $0<\phi<\alpha$, where $\alpha=\pi/N$ and $N$ is an integer at least $2$. Construct the full finite image system using rotations and reflections, prove that it grounds both faces, and count the images.

Then set $N=3$. Derive an exact expression for the physical interaction energy for general $0<\phi_0<\pi/3$, and simplify it on the bisector $\phi_0=\pi/6$. State why the energy, rather than $qV_{\rm image}$, contains a factor of one-half.
permittedResults: Two points at the same radius $\rho$ and angular separation $\Delta\phi$ are separated by $2\rho|\sin(\Delta\phi/2)|$.
Grounded image energy is $qV_{\rm image}/2$.
problems.strategy: Generate an even rotational orbit of positive charges and its reflected negative orbit, pair contributions on each face, then use chord lengths to sum the $N=3$ image potential.
hints: Use $+q$ at $\phi_0+2k\alpha$ and $-q$ at $-\phi_0+2k\alpha$ for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$.
Remove only the $k=0$ positive charge from the image sum.
For $N=3$, the two positive images are each a distance $\sqrt3\rho$ away.
problems.solution:
Take the $2N$-charge orbit
$$+q:\ \phi=\phi_0+2k\alpha,\qquad -q:\ \phi=-\phi_0+2k\alpha, \qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.$$
The $k=0$ positive member is the real charge, leaving $2N-1$ images. Reflection pairs have equal distance and opposite sign on $\phi=0$; after a rotation-index shift the same is true on $\phi=\alpha$. Thus both wedge faces are grounded.

For $N=3$, the two positive images contribute $2/(\sqrt3\rho)$ to $V_{\rm image}/(k_eq)$. The three negative images have distances $2\rho|\sin(k\pi/3-\phi_0)|$. Therefore
$$\boxed{U(\phi_0)=\frac{k_eq^2}{4\rho}\left[\frac4{\sqrt3}- \sum_{k=0}^2\frac1{|\sin(k\pi/3-\phi_0)|}\right]}.$$
On the bisector the three cosecant magnitudes are $2,2,1$, so
$$\boxed{U(\pi/6)=\frac{k_eq^2}{4\rho}\left(\frac4{\sqrt3}-5\right)}.$$
The factor $1/2$ accounts for the gradual work required to build the induced conductor charge; the image potential itself already gives the full physical force field at the real charge.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the two finite charge orbits, counts $2N-1$ images, and proves both boundary cancellations.
Uses chord distances and the physical one-half factor to obtain the general $N=3$ energy.
Simplifies the bisector sum correctly and explains the energy-factor origin.

commonErrors.description: Stops after a single reflection in each wedge face.
commonErrors.consequence: Repeated reflections fail to close and one boundary is regrounded only at the expense of the other.

commonErrors.description: Includes the real $+q$ member in $V_{\rm image}$ or omits the physical one-half factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy is divergent or double-counted.

problems.flawedProof: Two negative mirror charges, one in each face, always ground a wedge. For $N=3$ their energy is $q$ times the two-image potential; the other rotations merely duplicate the same field and may be omitted.

problems.title: Separate eccentric cylinders in a bipolar coordinate strip
problems.objective: Use bipolar coordinates to derive the capacitance of nested nonconcentric cylinders and recover both concentric and near-contact limits.
problems.statement:
An infinite conducting cylinder of radius $a$ is held at $V_0$ inside a grounded cylinder of radius $b>a$. Their axes are parallel and their center separation is $c$, where $0\le c<b-a$. In bipolar coordinates $(\tau,\sigma)$ the two circular boundaries are $\tau=\tau_1$ and $\tau=\tau_2$, with $\Delta\tau=\tau_1-\tau_2>0$, and the common scale factor is
$$h_\tau=h_\sigma=\frac{s}{\cosh\tau-\cos\sigma}.$$
You may use the geometric relation
$$\cosh\Delta\tau=\frac{b^2+a^2-c^2}{2ab}.$$
Find the potential, integrate the inner-cylinder charge per unit length, and derive $C/L$. Check the limits $c\to0$ and $c\to(b-a)^-$, including the physical direction of the capacitance change.
permittedResults: The bipolar-coordinate scale factor and circle-separation relation are supplied.
$\operatorname{arcosh}[(x+x^{-1})/2]=|\ln x|$ for $x>0$.
problems.strategy: Solve the strip problem linearly in $\tau$, use cancellation of the metric factor in $E_n dl$, and translate the strip width into physical radii and offset only at the end.
hints: The boundary values make $V$ affine in $\tau$.
On the inner boundary, $|E_n|=V_0/(h_\tau\Delta\tau)$ and $dl=h_\sigma d\sigma$.
Internal tangency sends the arcosh argument to one.
problems.solution:
The unique harmonic strip solution is
$$\boxed{V(\tau)=V_0\frac{\tau-\tau_2}{\Delta\tau}}.$$
The field points from the inner conductor into the dielectric. Because the two scale factors agree,
$$\frac QL=\int_0^{2\pi}\epsilon\frac{V_0}{h_\tau\Delta\tau}h_\sigma d\sigma =\frac{2\pi\epsilon V_0}{\Delta\tau}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\frac CL=\frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left[(b^2+a^2-c^2)/(2ab)\right]}}.$$
When $c=0$, the arcosh is $\ln(b/a)$ and the familiar coaxial result $C/L=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)$ is recovered. As $c\to(b-a)^-$, the arcosh argument approaches $1^+$, so $\Delta\tau\to0$ and $C/L\to\infty$. The narrowing local gap strengthens charge storage at fixed voltage, so the increasing capacitance has the correct physical direction.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the affine bipolar-coordinate potential and invokes uniqueness.
Integrates the surface charge with the two metric factors correctly canceled.
Obtains the eccentric capacitance formula and verifies both concentric and near-contact limits.

commonErrors.description: Leaves an uncanceled scale factor in the charge integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The result depends spuriously on $\sigma$ and does not reduce to a simple strip width.

commonErrors.description: Uses $b^2+a^2+c^2$ in the arcosh argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted capacitance decreases and remains finite at internal tangency.

problems.flawedProof: The coordinate strip has constant field $V_0/\Delta\tau$, so its circumference is simply $2\pi a$ and $C/L=2\pi\epsilon a/\Delta\tau$. Increasing eccentricity increases the arcosh argument and therefore lowers the capacitance.

problems.title: Integrate a dipolar volume charge with the grounded-sphere Green function
problems.objective: Construct the Dirichlet Green function by Kelvin inversion and use its harmonic expansion to integrate a nonspherical source exactly.
problems.statement:
Inside a grounded spherical cavity $r<a$, use the convention
$$\nabla^2G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),\qquad G=0\ \text{at }r=a.$$
Construct $G$ using the Kelvin image of a unit source at $\mathbf r'$, and verify both its boundary value and source normalization. Then use
$$\rho(r',\theta')=\rho_0\frac{r'}a\cos\theta'$$
throughout the cavity to evaluate
$$V(\mathbf r)=\frac1{\epsilon_0}\int_{r'<a}G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')\rho(\mathbf r')d\tau'.$$
You may expand $G$ in Legendre polynomials. Verify Poisson's equation, regularity at the center, and the grounded boundary.
permittedResults: The Coulomb kernel has expansion $|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^{-1}=\sum_l r_<^l r_>^{-l-1}P_l(\cos\gamma)$.
$\int P_l(\cos\gamma)\cos\theta' d\Omega'=(4\pi/3)\cos\theta\,\delta_{l1}$.
problems.strategy: Write the inverted-source Green function, expand it so the angular integral selects only $l=1$, and split the remaining radial integral at $r'=r$.
hints: The image point is $\mathbf r_i'=(a^2/r'^2)\mathbf r'$ with strength factor $-a/r'$.
The $l=1$ radial kernel is $r_</r_>^2-rr'/a^3$.
After angular integration, evaluate the ranges $0<r'<r$ and $r<r'<a$ separately.
problems.solution:
Kelvin inversion gives
$$\boxed{G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\frac1{4\pi}\left[ \frac1{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}-\frac a{r'} \frac1{|\mathbf r-(a^2/r'^2)\mathbf r'|}\right]}.$$
The second source lies outside the cavity, so it is harmonic inside; the first term has the required $-\delta$ normalization. The Kelvin distance identity makes the bracket vanish at $r=a$.

Its interior expansion is
$$G=\frac1{4\pi}\sum_{l=0}^\infty\left[ \frac{r_<^l}{r_>^{l+1}}-\frac{(rr')^l}{a^{2l+1}}\right]P_l(\cos\gamma).$$
The angular integral selects $l=1$, leaving
$$V=\frac{\rho_0\cos\theta}{3\epsilon_0a} \int_0^a r'^3\left(\frac{r_<}{r_>^2}-\frac{rr'}{a^3}\right)dr'.$$
Splitting at $r$ gives the radial integral $3(a^2r-r^3)/10$. Thus
$$\boxed{V(r,\theta)=\frac{\rho_0}{10\epsilon_0a}(a^2r-r^3)\cos\theta}.$$
For $f(r)\cos\theta$, the radial Laplacian operator sends $r^3\cos\theta$ to $10r\cos\theta$ and annihilates $r\cos\theta$, so $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0$. The solution is regular at $r=0$ and vanishes at $r=a$.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the Kelvin Green function with the correct image point, coefficient, and normalization.
Uses the Legendre selection rule and evaluates the split radial integral correctly.
Obtains the closed potential and independently verifies Poisson's equation, regularity, and boundary data.

commonErrors.description: Places the Kelvin image at $(a/r')\mathbf r'$ or omits its factor $a/r'$.
commonErrors.consequence: The Green function does not vanish on the entire spherical boundary.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only the direct $l=1$ kernel and drops the boundary subtraction.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting potential fails the grounded condition at $r=a$.

problems.flawedProof: A grounded sphere needs an equal negative source at $a^2\mathbf r'/r'^2$, so the coefficient is always $-1$. Only the direct Coulomb term contributes to a volume integral because the image is outside, yielding a nonzero boundary voltage.

problems.title: Reconstruct a three-conductor Maxwell matrix and expose its gauge mode
problems.objective: Recover a capacitance matrix from voltage experiments, prove its positive-semidefinite energy form, and compute a gauge-invariant test case.
problems.statement:
Three isolated conductors form a closed electrostatic system. Charges and voltages obey $\mathbf Q=C\mathbf V$, where the Maxwell capacitance matrix is symmetric and every row sum is zero. Two one-volt experiments produce
$$\mathbf V^{(1)}=(1,0,0),\quad \mathbf Q^{(1)}=(3,-2,-1)\ \mathrm{nC},$$
$$\mathbf V^{(2)}=(0,1,0),\quad \mathbf Q^{(2)}=(-2,5,-3)\ \mathrm{nC}.$$
Reconstruct the full matrix in nanofarads. Express $\tfrac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V$ as a sum of nonnegative pair-voltage terms and identify the complete nullspace. For $\mathbf V=(4,-1,2)\,\mathrm V$, find all charges and the energy. Finally add $6\,\mathrm V$ to every conductor and verify what changes.
permittedResults: Reciprocity makes $C$ symmetric, and a uniform voltage shift leaves all charges unchanged in a closed system.
problems.strategy: Read the first two experimental columns, use symmetry and row sums to reconstruct the third, then rewrite the quadratic form using pairwise differences.
hints: The experimental charge vectors are columns of $C$.
The third entry in each row is fixed by the zero row sum.
Look for pair coefficients $2$, $1$, and $3$ nanofarads.
problems.solution:
The experiments give the first two columns; symmetry and zero row sums complete the matrix:
$$\boxed{C=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2&-1\\-2&5&-3\\-1&-3&4\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{nF}}.$$
Its energy is
$$\boxed{U=\frac12\left[2(V_1-V_2)^2+(V_1-V_3)^2+3(V_2-V_3)^2\right]\ \mathrm{nJ}},$$
when voltages are in volts. This is nonnegative. It vanishes only when $V_1=V_2=V_3$, so the nullspace is exactly the uniform gauge vector $\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)\}$.

For $(4,-1,2)$,
$$\boxed{\mathbf Q=(12,-19,7)\ \mathrm{nC}},$$
whose entries sum to zero, and
$$U=\frac12[2(5)^2+(2)^2+3(-3)^2]=\boxed{40.5\ \mathrm{nJ}}.$$
Adding six volts gives $(10,5,8)$ but preserves every voltage difference. Because $C(1,1,1)^T=0$, the charges and energy are unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Reconstructs every matrix entry from the two columns, symmetry, and row-sum constraint.
Rewrites the quadratic form as nonnegative pair terms and identifies exactly the uniform nullspace.
Computes the test charges and energy and verifies invariance under a common voltage shift.

commonErrors.description: Treats the experimental charge vectors as rows while ignoring reciprocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed matrix is asymmetric or conflicts with the measured second experiment.

commonErrors.description: Declares the full matrix positive definite.
commonErrors.consequence: The unavoidable uniform-voltage gauge null vector is missed.

problems.flawedProof: The two experiments determine only six unrelated entries, so set the third column to zero. All diagonal entries are positive, which proves positive definiteness; adding six volts must therefore add charge to every conductor.

problems.title: Differentiate Dirichlet energy into Maxwell boundary pressure
problems.objective: Derive the first shape variation of electrostatic field energy and verify its sign on a movable parallel plate.
problems.statement:
A charge-free dielectric region $\Omega$ has permittivity $\epsilon$ and electrostatic potential $V$ with fixed constant values on its conducting boundary components. Let a smooth conducting boundary piece $\Gamma$ move by normal displacement $\xi(\mathbf x)$ along the unit normal $\mathbf n$ pointing outward from the dielectric region. Denote the Eulerian shape derivative of the potential at fixed reference coordinates by $\dot V$; this is distinct from the material derivative following a moving boundary point.

Show that fixed boundary voltage implies $\dot V=-\xi\partial_nV$ on $\Gamma$, and derive the Hadamard variation
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma(\partial_nV)^2\xi\,da.$$
Interpret the result as Maxwell pressure. Check the sign and magnitude for parallel plates of area $A$, separation $d$, and voltage difference $V_0$ when the upper plate moves by $\delta d>0$. State the smooth-boundary assumptions under which the derivation is valid.
permittedResults: The transport rule adds $\int_\Gamma f\xi da$ when a domain boundary moves outward.
The unperturbed and material-derivative potentials are harmonic in the charge-free region.
problems.strategy: Differentiate both the boundary condition and the volume energy, integrate the cross term by parts, and combine it with the moving-domain term before interpreting signs.
hints: Differentiate $V(\mathbf x+\xi\mathbf n)=V_{\rm conductor}$.
On an equipotential conductor, $|\nabla V|^2=(\partial_nV)^2$.
For the upper parallel plate, the dielectric outward normal is $+\hat z$ and the electrical force on that plate points in $-\hat z$.
problems.solution:
Differentiating the fixed boundary value along the moving surface yields
$$\boxed{\dot V+\xi\partial_nV=0\quad\text{on }\Gamma}.$$
For $U_{\rm field}=\frac\epsilon2\int_\Omega|\nabla V|^2d\tau$, the transport and field variations give
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=\epsilon\int_\Omega\nabla V\cdot\nabla\dot Vd\tau +\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma|\nabla V|^2\xi da.$$
Integration by parts removes the volume term because $\nabla^2V=0$, leaving $\epsilon\int_\Gamma\dot V\partial_nVda$. Substitution of the boundary derivative and use of zero tangential field give
$$\boxed{\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma(\partial_nV)^2\xi da}.$$
Thus the Maxwell pressure magnitude is $p=\epsilon E_n^2/2$, and the traction on the conductor is $-p\mathbf n$: it points into the dielectric.

For parallel plates, $U_{\rm field}=\epsilon AV_0^2/(2d)$, so
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac{\epsilon AV_0^2}{2d^2}\delta d=-pA\delta d,$$
with $p=\epsilon V_0^2/(2d^2)$. The upper plate is pulled downward, opposite its positive displacement. The derivation assumes a smooth displacement, a smooth equipotential surface, no edge or corner singular contribution, and no topology change.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the moving fixed-potential boundary to obtain the correct Eulerian shape-derivative boundary data.
Combines integration by parts with the domain-transport term to derive the exact one-half coefficient and sign.
Interprets the traction and verifies it against the parallel-plate energy, including scope assumptions.

commonErrors.description: Sets $\dot V=0$ on the reference boundary because the conductor voltage is fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The geometric change of the boundary condition is omitted and the shape derivative has the wrong coefficient.

commonErrors.description: Reports pressure $\epsilon E_n^2$ without the one-half or directs it out of the dielectric.
commonErrors.consequence: The result disagrees with the parallel-plate energy derivative and force direction.

problems.flawedProof: Fixed voltage gives $\dot V=0$, so only the transported volume contributes and $\delta U=(\epsilon/2)\int E^2\xi da>0$. Therefore the electric pressure is outward and separates the plates.

problems.title: Optimize a two-parameter Rayleigh-Ritz capacitance bound
problems.objective: Minimize a coupled trial-energy quadratic, prove the stationary point is global, and combine it with a dual flux bound.
problems.statement:
A long two-conductor capacitor has a square grounded outer shield and a centered diamond-shaped inner conductor at voltage $V_0$. A boundary-conforming finite-element interpolation on one symmetry cell has been assembled as
$$u_t=g+\alpha f_1+\beta f_2,$$
where $u_t=1$ on the inner conductor and $u_t=0$ on the shield for every $\alpha,\beta$. After exact cell integration and symmetry restoration, its Dirichlet functional is
$$\frac{C_t/L}{\epsilon}=J(\alpha,\beta) =5+4\alpha^2+6\beta^2+2\alpha\beta-4\alpha+2\beta.$$
Find the optimal parameters and the certified upper bound on $C/L$. Prove the stationary point is the unique global minimizer, compare it with the best one-parameter restriction $\beta=0$, and combine it with an independently admissible normalized-flux trial giving $C/L\ge3.40\epsilon$. Explain why changing the overall geometric scale does not change these two-dimensional per-length coefficients.
permittedResults: A boundary-admissible potential gives $C/L\le C_t/L$ at fixed voltage.
A positive-definite quadratic has a unique global minimizer.
problems.strategy: Solve the coupled normal equations, certify the Hessian rather than assuming stationarity is enough, and compare nested trial spaces before adding the independent lower bound.
hints: The normal equations are $4\alpha+\beta=2$ and $\alpha+6\beta=-1$.
The Hessian is $\begin{pmatrix}8&2\\2&12\end{pmatrix}$.
For $\beta=0$, minimize a single completed square.
problems.solution:
The normal equations give
$$\boxed{\alpha=\frac{13}{23},\qquad\beta=-\frac6{23}}.$$
The Hessian has leading minor $8>0$ and determinant $92>0$, so it is positive definite and this stationary point is the unique global minimizer. Substitution gives
$$J_{\min}=\frac{1909}{529}=3.60869\ldots,$$
and therefore
$$\boxed{\frac CL\le\frac{1909}{529}\epsilon\approx3.609\epsilon}.$$
If $\beta=0$, then $J=5+4\alpha^2-4\alpha$ is minimized at $\alpha=1/2$, giving $J=4$. Thus the enlarged trial space improves the upper bound, as it must. With the dual trial,
$$\boxed{3.40\epsilon\le\frac CL\le3.609\epsilon}.$$
Under a uniform rescaling of a two-dimensional cross-section, $|\nabla u|^2$ scales as length$^{-2}$ while $dA$ scales as length$^2$. Their product, and hence the dimensionless coefficient multiplying $\epsilon$, is scale invariant.
rubricCriteria: Solves the coupled normal equations and evaluates the exact minimized functional.
Uses positive definiteness to certify the unique global minimum and correctly compares the restricted trial space.
States the two-sided bound and explains the two-dimensional scale invariance.

commonErrors.description: Minimizes in $\alpha$ and $\beta$ independently while dropping the cross term.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed parameters do not satisfy the coupled stationarity equations.

commonErrors.description: Treats a trial potential as a lower bound on capacitance.
commonErrors.consequence: The final variational bracket is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: Set $\alpha=1/2$ and $\beta=-1/6$ by minimizing the square terms separately. Because the exact field has least energy, its capacitance must exceed the trial value, so $C/L\ge J\epsilon$ and the flux result is an upper bound.

problems.title: Map an offset cylinder above a plane into a strip
problems.objective: Derive the cylinder-plane capacitance by a conformal strip coordinate and resolve its near-contact charge crowding.
problems.statement:
An infinite conducting cylinder of radius $a$ has its axis a height $h>a$ above a grounded plane and is held at voltage $V_0$. Let $s=\sqrt{h^2-a^2}$ and use bipolar coordinates
$$x=\frac{s\sin\sigma}{\cosh\tau-\cos\sigma},\qquad y=\frac{s\sinh\tau}{\cosh\tau-\cos\sigma}.$$
This conformal map sends the plane to $\tau=0$ and the cylinder to $\tau=\tau_0$, where $\cosh\tau_0=h/a$; its scale factor is $H=s/(\cosh\tau-\cos\sigma)$. Find $V$, the charge per unit length, and $C/L$. Determine the surface-field maximum and analyze both $g=h-a\ll a$ and $h\gg a$. Explain the incipient cusp behavior as the cylinder approaches contact.
permittedResults: The stated bipolar map is conformal with equal scale factors.
$\operatorname{arcosh}(1+x)\sim\sqrt{2x}$ for $x\downarrow0$.
problems.strategy: Solve linearly across the conformal strip, cancel the metric factors in the charge integral, then retain the metric locally to locate and scale the crowded field.
hints: Use $V=V_0\tau/\tau_0$.
The closest cylinder point corresponds to $\sigma=\pi$.
For small gap, $s\sim\sqrt{2ag}$ and $\tau_0\sim\sqrt{2g/a}$.
problems.solution:
The strip solution and capacitance are
$$\boxed{V=V_0\frac\tau{\tau_0}},\qquad \frac QL=\int_0^{2\pi}\epsilon\frac{V_0}{H\tau_0}H\,d\sigma =\frac{2\pi\epsilon V_0}{\tau_0},$$
$$\boxed{\frac CL=\frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\operatorname{arcosh}(h/a)}}.$$
On the cylinder,
$$|E_n(\sigma)|=\frac{V_0}{H\tau_0} =\frac{V_0(\cosh\tau_0-\cos\sigma)}{s\tau_0}.$$
It is maximal at the closest point $\sigma=\pi$:
$$\boxed{E_{\max}=\frac{V_0(\cosh\tau_0+1)}{s\tau_0}}.$$
For $g=h-a\ll a$, $s\sim\sqrt{2ag}$ and $\tau_0\sim\sqrt{2g/a}$, so
$$\frac CL\sim\sqrt2\pi\epsilon\sqrt{\frac ag},\qquad E_{\max}\sim\frac{V_0}{g}.$$
The capacitance and local field diverge as the smooth gap collapses into a tangential-contact cusp. For $h\gg a$, $\tau_0\sim\ln(2h/a)$ and $C/L\sim2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2h/a)$, which decreases as the return conductor recedes.
rubricCriteria: Uses the conformal strip coordinate to construct the potential and integrate the exact capacitance.
Retains the local scale factor to locate and compute the maximum surface field.
Derives the small-gap and far-separation asymptotics and interprets the incipient cusp singularity.

commonErrors.description: Uses the constant strip derivative $V_0/\tau_0$ as the physical field without dividing by $H$.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge crowding and the near-gap divergence are missed.

commonErrors.description: Expands $\operatorname{arcosh}(1+g/a)$ linearly in $g/a$.
commonErrors.consequence: The capacitance is assigned an incorrect $1/g$ rather than $1/\sqrt g$ divergence.

problems.flawedProof: Conformal maps preserve physical distances, so the field is uniform and equals $V_0/\tau_0$. Since $\operatorname{arcosh}(1+x)\sim x$, both the capacitance and field diverge as $1/g$ everywhere on the cylinder.

problems.title: Build a mixed-boundary Green function and reconcile its corners and energy
problems.objective: Construct a Dirichlet-Neumann Green series, derive the full representation formula, and connect corner compatibility to the energy identity.
problems.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,L)\times(0,H)$. Impose Dirichlet data on $x=0$, $x=L$, and $y=H$, and outward-normal Neumann data on $y=0$. For the homogeneous mixed Green function use
$$\nabla^2G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),$$
with $G=0$ on the Dirichlet pieces and $\partial_nG=0$ on the bottom.

Construct $G$ as a normalized double eigenfunction series and prove symmetry. Then derive the representation of a Poisson solution $-\epsilon\nabla^2V=\rho$ with Dirichlet value $f$ and bottom flux $g=\partial_nV$. State the classical corner compatibility conditions at the two bottom corners. Finally derive the energy identity and specialize it to homogeneous boundary data to prove uniqueness and positivity.
permittedResults: Green's second identity and orthogonality of sine and cosine eigenfunctions may be used.
$\int_0^L\sin^2(n\pi x/L)dx=L/2$ and $\int_0^H\cos^2((m+1/2)\pi y/H)dy=H/2$.
problems.strategy: Match each homogeneous edge with an eigenfunction parity, normalize the delta expansion, then derive representation and energy formulas with boundary signs kept symbolic until the end.
hints: Use $\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\mu_my)$ with $\mu_m=(m+1/2)\pi/H$.
On a Dirichlet edge $G=0$; on the Neumann edge $\partial_nG=0$.
At $(0,0)$, outward bottom data satisfy $g(0)=-\partial_yV(0,0)=-f_L'(0)$.
problems.solution:
Set $k_n=n\pi/L$ and $\mu_m=(m+1/2)\pi/H$. The normalized Green function is
$$\boxed{G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\frac4{LH}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{\sin(k_nx)\sin(k_nx')\cos(\mu_my)\cos(\mu_my')} {k_n^2+\mu_m^2}}.$$
It has the required zero values and zero bottom normal derivative; applying $-\nabla^2$ produces the mixed delta expansion. Every term is symmetric under $\mathbf r\leftrightarrow\mathbf r'$, so $G$ is symmetric.

Green's identity gives
$$\boxed{V(\mathbf r)=\frac1\epsilon\int_\Omega G\rho\,dA' -\int_{\Gamma_D}f\,\partial_{n'}G\,ds' +\int_{y'=0}Gg\,dx'}.$$
If the side data are $f_L(y)$ and $f_R(y)$, classical $C^1$ compatibility at the bottom corners requires
$$\boxed{g(0)=-f_L'(0),\qquad g(L)=-f_R'(0)}.$$
Failure need not destroy a weak solution, but it produces a corner singularity and prevents the claimed classical regularity.

Multiplying $-\epsilon\nabla^2V=\rho$ by $V$ and integrating yields
$$\boxed{\epsilon\int_\Omega|\nabla V|^2dA =\int_\Omega\rho VdA+\epsilon\int_{\partial\Omega}V\partial_nVds}.$$
For homogeneous mixed data the boundary term vanishes, so $\epsilon\int|\nabla V|^2=\int\rho V$. With $\rho=0$, the gradient vanishes; the nonempty Dirichlet boundary then fixes the remaining constant to zero, proving uniqueness. The same identity gives nonnegative field energy $U=(1/2)\int\rho V$ for homogeneous data.
rubricCriteria: Constructs and normalizes the mixed eigenfunction Green series and proves its symmetry.
Derives the source and both boundary terms with correct signs and states both corner compatibility conditions.
Obtains the energy identity and uses homogeneous data to prove uniqueness and positivity.

commonErrors.description: Uses sine modes in $y$ and therefore imposes Dirichlet rather than Neumann data at the bottom.
commonErrors.consequence: The Green function solves a different boundary-value problem.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Neumann boundary term from the representation because $\partial_nG=0$ there.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor that vanishes is confused with $G$, so prescribed bottom flux has no effect.

problems.flawedProof: Use sines in both coordinates so every edge is Dirichlet. The bottom term vanishes because Green functions are zero on all boundaries, and mixed corner data never need compatibility. Positivity follows even if the Green series has the wrong boundary type.

problems.title: Renormalize an infinite image group into a finite self-energy
problems.objective: Extract the regular part of a parallel-plate Green function, express it with digamma functions, and obtain the exact force and stability.
problems.statement:
A charge $q$ lies at height $z_0$ between grounded planes $z=0$ and $z=L$. Reflections in the two planes generate an infinite dihedral image group. With $\rho^2=(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2$, use
$$G=\frac1{4\pi}\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\left[ \frac1{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z-z_0-2nL)^2}}- \frac1{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z+z_0-2nL)^2}}\right].$$
Verify the group interpretation and boundary values. Define
$$H(z_0)=\lim_{\mathbf r\to\mathbf r_0}\left[G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r_0)-\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}\right].$$
Using symmetric summation and $x=z_0/L$, show
$$H=\frac{\psi(x)+\psi(1-x)+2\gamma}{8\pi L},$$
then find the renormalized physical energy and force. Check the midplane and one-wall limits and classify the midplane equilibrium.
permittedResults: Reflections in $z=0$ and $z=L$ generate translations by $2L$.
$\psi(x)+\psi(1-x)+2\gamma$ equals the symmetrically convergent harmonic-series difference arising here.
$\psi_1(x)\sim x^{-2}$ as $x\downarrow0$.
problems.strategy: Remove only the real-source singular term, pair the remote images before taking the coincidence limit, and differentiate the already-renormalized physical energy.
hints: The positive translated sources are at $z_0+2nL$ and the negative reflected sources at $-z_0+2nL$.
At coincidence, the paired dimensionless sum is $2\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-1}-x^{-1}-\sum_{n\ge1}[(n-x)^{-1}+(n+x)^{-1}]$.
Use $U=q^2H/(2\epsilon_0)$, not $q^2H/\epsilon_0$.
problems.solution:
The two generating reflections produce the translated positive orbit $z_0+2nL$ and reflected negative orbit $-z_0+2nL$. Reindexing cancels the series at each plane. Symmetric pairing makes the remote $1/|n|$ pieces cancel before the coincidence limit.

Removing the $n=0$ positive singularity gives
$$H=\frac1{8\pi L}\left[2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1n-\frac1x- \sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac1{n-x}+\frac1{n+x}\right)\right],$$
which is the stated digamma form. Therefore
$$\boxed{U(z_0)=\frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0L} [\psi(x)+\psi(1-x)+2\gamma]}.$$
Differentiation yields
$$\boxed{F_z=-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0L^2} [\psi_1(x)-\psi_1(1-x)]}.$$
At $x=1/2$, symmetry makes $F_z=0$. A small upward displacement makes the nearer upper wall attract more strongly, so the midpoint is an unstable energy maximum. As $z_0\downarrow0$,
$$U\sim-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0z_0},\qquad F_z\sim-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0z_0^2},$$
exactly the grounded-plane energy and force. The corresponding upper-wall limit follows by $z_0\mapsto L-z_0$.
rubricCriteria: Identifies the reflection-generated image orbits and verifies both grounded boundaries with symmetric summation.
Subtracts the correct Coulomb singularity and converts the finite paired sum to the stated regular part.
Uses the physical one-half factor, differentiates to the trigamma force, and checks symmetry, stability, and one-wall limits.

commonErrors.description: Sums the two divergent harmonic series separately before subtracting them.
commonErrors.consequence: The regular part is assigned an ordering-dependent infinite value.

commonErrors.description: Uses $q^2H/\epsilon_0$ as the physical energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy and force are both twice the grounded-plane limit.

problems.flawedProof: The positive and negative image sums each diverge, so their difference is infinite and no force exists. If one simply drops all divergent terms, the energy is $q^2H/\epsilon_0$ and the midplane is stable because the two attractions cancel there.

problems.title: Partition battery work and force in a moving three-conductor system
problems.objective: Use a shape derivative of a singular capacitance matrix to compute fixed-voltage force, battery work, fixed-charge agreement, and gauge invariance.
problems.statement:
Three conductors have Maxwell capacitance matrix $C(s)=C_0+sC_1+O(s^2)$, where positive $s$ is a specified mechanical displacement measured in millimeters,
$$C_0=\begin{pmatrix}5&-2&-3\\-2&6&-4\\-3&-4&7\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{nF},\qquad C_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&3&-2\\0&-2&2\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{nF/mm}.$$
Ideal voltage sources hold $\mathbf V=(5,1,-2)\,\mathrm V$ while $s$ increases. Verify the structural constraints on $C_0$ and $C_1$. Compute $d\mathbf Q/ds$, $dU_{\rm field}/ds$, the generalized mechanical force, and the battery work per displacement. Reconcile their factors of two by energy conservation.

Then disconnect the sources while retaining the instantaneous charges. Show that the fixed-charge energy derivative gives the same instantaneous force. Finally prove that adding any common voltage to $\mathbf V$ changes none of these results.
permittedResults: At fixed voltages, $U_{\rm field}=\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V$ and source work is $\delta W_{\rm batt}=\mathbf V^T\delta\mathbf Q$.
At fixed charges on a referenced subspace, $U_Q=\frac12\mathbf Q^TC^{-1}\mathbf Q$.
problems.strategy: Exploit row sums before multiplying, distinguish field energy from the voltage-source work, and differentiate the inverse matrix only on the gauge-fixed charge subspace.
hints: Both matrices are symmetric and annihilate $(1,1,1)^T$.
$\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=(V_1-V_2)^2+2(V_2-V_3)^2$.
Use $dC^{-1}/ds=-C^{-1}C_1C^{-1}$ after fixing a reference.
problems.solution:
Both matrices are symmetric, have positive diagonal and nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and every row sum is zero. Thus the uniform gauge mode persists to first order. Direct multiplication gives
$$\boxed{\frac{d\mathbf Q}{ds}=C_1\mathbf V=(4,2,-6)\ \mathrm{nC/mm}},$$
whose entries sum to zero. At fixed voltage,
$$\frac{dU_{\rm field}}{ds}=\frac12\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V =\frac12[4^2+2(3)^2]=\boxed{17\ \mathrm{nJ/mm}}.$$
The fixed-voltage electromechanical force is the coenergy derivative,
$$\boxed{F_s=+\frac12\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=17\ \mathrm{\mu N}},$$
because $1\,\mathrm{nJ/mm}=1\,\mathrm{\mu N}$. The sources supply
$$\frac{dW_{\rm batt}}{ds}=\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=\boxed{34\ \mathrm{nJ/mm}}.$$
Half is stored in the stronger field and half is delivered as mechanical work: $dW_{\rm batt}=dU_{\rm field}+F_sds$.

After disconnection, $U_Q=\frac12\mathbf Q^TC^{-1}\mathbf Q$ on any gauge-fixed two-dimensional subspace. Since $\mathbf V=C^{-1}\mathbf Q$ there,
$$\left.\frac{dU_Q}{ds}\right|_{\mathbf Q}=-\frac12\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=-17\ \mathrm{nJ/mm},$$
so $F_s=-dU_Q/ds=17\,\mathrm{\mu N}$ at that instant. Finally, $C_1\mathbf1=0$ implies $(\mathbf V+v_g\mathbf1)^TC_1(\mathbf V+v_g\mathbf1)=\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V$ and $C_1(\mathbf V+v_g\mathbf1)=C_1\mathbf V$. Charge change, work, and force are all gauge invariant.
rubricCriteria: Verifies symmetry and gauge row sums and computes the charge derivative with zero total charge.
Separates fixed-voltage field-energy change, mechanical force, and twice-as-large battery work with a correct conservation statement.
Derives fixed-charge agreement on a gauge-fixed subspace and proves invariance under common voltage shifts.

commonErrors.description: Uses $-\frac12\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V$ as the fixed-voltage force by applying the isolated-system rule while sources remain attached.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted force points opposite the capacitance-increasing displacement.

commonErrors.description: Equates all battery work with field-energy change and omits mechanical work.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor of two is treated as a contradiction rather than an energy partition.

problems.flawedProof: Because force is always minus the derivative of $\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V$, the force is $-17\,\mu\mathrm N$. The batteries supply only $17\,\mathrm{nJ/mm}$, and adding a common voltage changes the quadratic form because each diagonal entry is positive.

problems.title: Solve a multiply connected capacitor by modulus, reciprocity, and uniqueness
problems.objective: Combine conformal invariance, harmonic measure, reciprocity, and an energy proof in a doubly connected electrostatic domain.
problems.statement:
A long two-dimensional capacitor has a doubly connected dielectric cross-section $\Omega$ with inner conductor $A$ and outer conductor $B$. A known conformal map $w=f(z)$ sends $\Omega$ onto the annulus
$$1<|w|<R,\qquad R>1,$$
with $A$ mapped to $|w|=1$ and $B$ to $|w|=R$. First hold $A$ at $V_0$ and ground $B$. Find the potential in physical coordinates and derive $C/L$ by either charge integration or conformal invariance of Dirichlet energy.

Next ground both conductors and place a line charge of density $\lambda$ at $z_0\in\Omega$. Use a separate unit-voltage weighting problem and Green reciprocity to find the total induced charges on $A$ and $B$ without constructing the sourced Green function. Prove uniqueness even though the domain is multiply connected. Analyze the limits $z_0$ approaching either boundary, $R\downarrow1$ at fixed conformal fraction $t=\ln|f(z_0)|/\ln R$, and $R\to\infty$ with $|f(z_0)|$ fixed.
permittedResults: Two-dimensional Laplace equations and Dirichlet energy are conformally invariant.
Green reciprocity may be applied between the sourced grounded state and a source-free unit-voltage weighting state.
problems.strategy: Solve the annulus once to obtain its harmonic measure, reuse that function as the reciprocity weight, and close every result with an energy uniqueness argument and degeneration limits.
hints: The inner-conductor harmonic measure is $\omega_A(z)=\ln[R/|f(z)|]/\ln R$.
Reciprocity gives $Q_A/L=-\lambda\omega_A(z_0)$.
The two induced charges must sum to $-\lambda$.
problems.solution:
The annular Dirichlet solution pulls back to
$$\boxed{V(z)=V_0\frac{\ln[R/|f(z)|]}{\ln R}}.$$
On either circular image boundary, integrating $\epsilon E_n$ gives
$$\boxed{\frac CL=\frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\ln R}}.$$
This also follows because $\int|\nabla V|^2dA$ is unchanged by the conformal map.

Define the harmonic measure
$$\omega_A(z)=\frac{\ln[R/|f(z)|]}{\ln R},$$
equal to one on $A$ and zero on $B$. Apply reciprocity between the grounded state containing $\lambda$ and the source-free state with weighting voltage $\omega_A$. The volume-source term is $\lambda\omega_A(z_0)$ per length, while the conductor term is the grounded-state charge $Q_A/L$. Hence
$$\boxed{\frac{Q_A}{L}=-\lambda\omega_A(z_0)},\qquad \boxed{\frac{Q_B}{L}=-\lambda[1-\omega_A(z_0)]}.$$
The second result follows either from the complementary weight or total induced charge $-\lambda$.

If two scalar potentials have the same Dirichlet data, their difference $u$ is harmonic and zero on both boundary components. Green's first identity gives $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2dA=0$, so $u=0$. Multiply connectedness permits harmonic vector fields with circulation only if one abandons a single-valued electrostatic potential; it does not spoil this Dirichlet uniqueness.

As $z_0\to A$, $\omega_A\to1$ and $Q_A/L\to-\lambda$; as $z_0\to B$, the outer conductor receives all induced charge. If $R\downarrow1$ with $t=\ln|f(z_0)|/\ln R$ fixed, then $C/L\to\infty$ and $(Q_A,Q_B)/L\to[-\lambda(1-t),-\lambda t]$. If $R\to\infty$ with $|f(z_0)|$ fixed, $C/L\to0$ logarithmically while $\omega_A\to1$, so the receding outer boundary carries a vanishing share of the induced charge.
rubricCriteria: Pulls back the annular potential and derives capacitance from the conformal modulus.
Uses the harmonic measure in a distinct reciprocity experiment to partition both induced charges.
Proves multiply connected Dirichlet uniqueness and correctly evaluates all boundary and modulus limits.

commonErrors.description: Assumes multiply connectedness introduces an arbitrary additive harmonic function even with both boundary potentials fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonexistent nonuniqueness is added despite the energy identity.

commonErrors.description: Assigns $Q_A/L=-\lambda[1-\omega_A(z_0)]$.
commonErrors.consequence: A charge approaching the inner conductor is incorrectly predicted to induce its charge on the remote outer boundary.

problems.flawedProof: A hole makes Laplace's equation nonunique, so add any circulation field to the annular solution. Reciprocity then divides induced charge equally between both conductors, independent of position, and the capacitance grows as $\ln R$ when the outer boundary recedes.
